# 10. Content generation

Level generation decides where the player goes; content generation decides what they find there: the monsters and items, the names of people and places, the books on the shelves, the histories behind the ruins, the quests, the events and the puzzles. This chapter is about generating those things well. It matters to anyone making a roguelike because content is where a generator most easily produces a great deal of output that nobody notices, and where a small amount of well-shaped variation can make each run feel like a new world.

The talks approach the subject from two directions at once. One is the craft of the generator: how to author parts that combine, how to shape a distribution, how to give a generator knowledge of what its pieces mean. The other is the player's perception: whether a difference can be seen, whether it matters in play, and what players will read into output nobody intended. The chapter starts with the general questions of how much content to generate and how to make it distinct, moves through specific kinds of content (names, text, histories, systems, quests, events, puzzles), and ends where the talks end, with the meaning players make.

## In brief

- Mathematically distinct output is worthless if players cannot perceive the difference, so exaggerate the axes players see and make differences matter in play ([Max Kreminski 2018, 14:36](https://youtu.be/TvlZinAvpwg?t=876); [Bruno Dias 2016, 9:58](https://youtu.be/UGPkEWqwSAY?t=598); [Liza Knipscher 2025, 21:02](https://youtu.be/jBhcHdV5HHo?t=1262); [Isaac Karth 2019, 4:39](https://youtu.be/MHEkE7nPuZc?t=279)).
- Generating each attribute independently makes every place a sample of the same distribution; correlate attributes in bundles, or vary the structure at a higher level so each region has its own character ([Alex Byaly 2022, 4:24](https://youtu.be/otEv5dh2f4E?t=264); [Alex Byaly 2022, 6:12](https://youtu.be/otEv5dh2f4E?t=372); [Alex Byaly 2022, 7:09](https://youtu.be/otEv5dh2f4E?t=429); [Jason Grinblat 2017, 22:11](https://youtu.be/ClGAApZYIvI?t=1331); [Darius Kazemi 2017, 28:11](https://youtu.be/CLi4PWxDmAI?t=1691)).
- Memorable output needs a plain baseline with a rare tail: a few spiky outliers stand out only against many ordinary ones ([Cat Manning 2020, 16:20](https://youtu.be/q7E1N-fJnrA?t=980); [Elliot Trinidad 2023, 11:45](https://youtu.be/9yFferxbrBU?t=705); [Joe Sondow 2017, 3:54](https://youtu.be/4byHHDeVKoA?t=234); [Jon Perry 2025, 16:06](https://youtu.be/NlxGPKV0PrY?t=966); [Ada Null 2025, 9:24](https://youtu.be/VzoruhRyvqQ?t=564)).
- Procedural generation is not a force multiplier for cheap content: an engine needs enough authored, tagged material to feed it, and more output is not automatically better ([Bruno Dias 2016, 11:49](https://youtu.be/UGPkEWqwSAY?t=709); [Santiago Zapata 2016, 14:14](https://youtu.be/TMxzVy7-VYQ?t=854); [Rich Wilson 2021, 11:22](https://youtu.be/wtlLa7BGZcs?t=682); [Cole Wehrle 2025, 19:31](https://youtu.be/HgnvMBVKP0M?t=1171)).
- A narrower, themed generative space can beat a bigger one, because theme is what lets recombined pieces cohere and lets every output meet an authored standard ([Aaron A. Reed 2020, 12:39](https://youtu.be/x0Xh4oCX9t0?t=759); [Cole Wehrle 2025, 10:21](https://youtu.be/HgnvMBVKP0M?t=621); [Matt Carney 2026, 20:18](https://youtu.be/SU-VcmsOvZo?t=1218); [Bruno Dias 2016, 8:37](https://youtu.be/UGPkEWqwSAY?t=517)).
- Author content in structures a generator can multiply and read: tags, variants, explicit category matrices, and metadata on text fragments that turns trivial variation into characterization ([Patrick Kemp 2023, 5:57](https://youtu.be/rWPJ5fW1UH8?t=357); [Patrick Kemp 2023, 10:12](https://youtu.be/rWPJ5fW1UH8?t=612); [Jasper Cole 2023, 17:06](https://youtu.be/COeJTtSDd78?t=1026); [Leigh Alexander 2023, 28:40](https://youtu.be/NjYS8XmeaiY?t=1720); [Aaron A. Reed 2020, 17:30](https://youtu.be/x0Xh4oCX9t0?t=1050); [Kate Compton 2016, 26:15](https://youtu.be/isB82kORimk?t=1575)).
- Generated text can only say what its source says, so choosing and curating the corpus is perhaps the most important decision in generative text ([Everest Pipkin 2019, 9:11](https://youtu.be/IYNKs8vfocc?t=551); [Everest Pipkin 2019, 10:39](https://youtu.be/IYNKs8vfocc?t=639); [Everest Pipkin 2019, 15:40](https://youtu.be/IYNKs8vfocc?t=940); [Kate Compton 2016, 30:57](https://youtu.be/isB82kORimk?t=1857)).
- Design name generators for identity, not just variety: names from one culture should be internally cohesive and distinct from other cultures' names ([Sraëka-Lillian 2021, 4:05](https://youtu.be/XQKNwaCwD-I?t=245); [Mark R Johnson 2019, 12:53](https://youtu.be/qh9vyoMviJI?t=773); [Elliot Trinidad 2023, 21:31](https://youtu.be/9yFferxbrBU?t=1291)).
- Generated histories and puzzles pay off when they leave traces in the world that the player can find, cross-reference and act on ([Jason Grinblat et al. 2018, 13:19](https://youtu.be/owmGknfj6H4?t=799); [Jason Grinblat 2017, 12:13](https://youtu.be/ClGAApZYIvI?t=733); [Mark Johnson 2023, 25:00](https://youtu.be/RDWt6RGN9wM?t=1500); [Bjarke Alexander Larsen 2026, 4:43](https://youtu.be/gxXZRofE5dI?t=283)).
- Players attach to and read meaning into generated content from very little, whether or not you intended it, so plan for both the attachment and the unintended readings ([Elliot Trinidad 2023, 4:28](https://youtu.be/9yFferxbrBU?t=268); [Joel Clark 2020, 30:32](https://youtu.be/zO05p-e57AQ?t=1832); [Younès Rabii 2020, 8:01](https://youtu.be/s6Kxh_Zyiqs?t=481); [Darius Kazemi 2017, 32:32](https://youtu.be/CLi4PWxDmAI?t=1952)).

## Why generate content, and how much is enough

### What generation buys you

Joseph Hewitt frames procedural generation as a kind of stage illusion: it conjures worlds that technically do not exist, so the craft of misdirection, making the audience see what did not happen, is especially relevant to roguelike developers ([Joseph Hewitt 2024, 2:34](https://youtu.be/dCWWId16VAo?t=154)). That framing is useful because it puts the player's perception, not the generator's output, at the centre, and the rest of this chapter keeps returning to it.

Why reach for the illusion at all? Everest Pipkin lists the motives designers give for generative text: a greater capacity for surprise, systems that produce ideas humans would not, stories you can re-enter for a different experience, and, sometimes, the plain fact that writing code that writes is easier than writing everything yourself ([Everest Pipkin 2019, 5:03](https://youtu.be/IYNKs8vfocc?t=303)). Zack Johnson draws a related lesson from Kingdom of Loathing's hobo name generator: when a game asks players to do something very repetitive, generated variation gives them something to look forward to in the next fight beyond their stats going up ([Zack Johnson 2016, 9:23](https://youtu.be/jNUMRG_tvrY?t=563)).

Even content that looks hand-made can be broken down for generation. Phillip Daigle built Rogue's Gate on the experiment of procedurally generating Baldur's Gate: looked at closely, even a narrative-heavy RPG decomposes into components that could be generated ([Phillip Daigle 2020, 7:08](https://youtu.be/2C3w7-SU5ek?t=428)). Stella Mazeika's survey of game randomizers shows the range of what can vary in a fixed game: aesthetics such as dialogue and sprite swaps, enemy placement and skills, player abilities, generated maps, and above all the locations of key items, which reshape the space of the game because items like Link to the Past's hookshot gate whole areas ([Stella Mazeika 2019, 5:45](https://youtu.be/C7laugXEc9s?t=345)).

Content generation also has a longer lineage than Rogue's rooms. Santiago Zapata points to tabletop Dungeon Master kits that included tools for generating random adventures, covering setting, NPCs and everything else in an adventure, where Rogue only created nine rooms and connected them ([Santiago Zapata 2018, 6:11](https://youtu.be/ZMdxP7fO6wE?t=371)). And the early games leaned on borrowed content as well as generated content: Dan Stormont and Michael Howk note that Hack, like Rogue, took many monsters from Advanced Dungeons & Dragons, some with stat blocks copied verbatim from the Monster Manual ([Dan Stormont and Michael Howk 2026, 7:11:37](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=25897)).

### The volume argument

The central disagreement in these talks is about quantity. One camp says breadth is the point. George Moromisato argues that quantity can itself be quality: NetHack endures because of the sheer breadth of monsters, levels and things to do, growing from Rogue's 26 monsters to Hack's doubled set to NetHack's hundreds, while few people still play Rogue ([George Moromisato 2016, 25:05](https://youtu.be/QBZkvtGucBU?t=1505)). He contrasts this with Ultima, whose small monster set gets animation and carefully balanced stats; NetHack instead wants so many monsters that every run is different and you can always meet something new ([George Moromisato 2016, 8:42](https://youtu.be/QBZkvtGucBU?t=522)). Jon Perry's Mini and Max, in UFO 50, makes the same demand from the design side: its core promise is that you can shrink anywhere and find something, which forced him to build a long list of rewards he could hand out procedurally, some as small as an NPC sharing lore, and to fill the gaps that handcrafting could not ([Jon Perry 2025, 7:14](https://youtu.be/NlxGPKV0PrY?t=434)). Zapata's own failure is the negative case. His Carmen Sandiego-inspired Elite International Detective had a tested, stable engine but never got the database of countries, cities and clues it needed, and the play experience was poor ([Santiago Zapata 2016, 14:14](https://youtu.be/TMxzVy7-VYQ?t=854)). An engine without enough authored content to feed it is not a game.

The other camp warns against treating generation as a content multiplier. Bruno Dias says plainly that procedural generation is not a force multiplier for cheap content: assemblage prose needs comprehensive tagging and handwritten material, and its real value is surprise and replayability, letting players go in blind on each dive ([Bruno Dias 2016, 11:49](https://youtu.be/UGPkEWqwSAY?t=709)). Cole Wehrle goes further and argues that too much content works against the feeling of intention and makes a game feel arbitrary. Oath has about 260 cards per suit, but the play deck is only about 60 and largely persists between games, so players form relationships with particular cards; the hated Favorite Son stays in so they can plan around it next time ([Cole Wehrle 2025, 19:31](https://youtu.be/HgnvMBVKP0M?t=1171)). Rich Wilson, borrowing Chris Crawford's idea of process intensity (how much a program relies on processes rather than data), names the "threat of infinite content": being able to procedurally fill a warehouse with crates to search does not mean you should ([Rich Wilson 2021, 11:22](https://youtu.be/wtlLa7BGZcs?t=682)). Max Kreminski raises an ethical version of the worry, that generation is often used to let players churn through and discard endless content, which can feed an extractive, colonial mode of play, though it can equally create worlds that go on beyond the player's grasp ([Max Kreminski 2018, 12:19](https://youtu.be/TvlZinAvpwg?t=739)). And Pipkin observes that much generative text bores because its novelty fades like a tech demo; Markov chains used to be funny and are not any more, and computation cannot replace a missing argument or poetics ([Everest Pipkin 2019, 15:00](https://youtu.be/IYNKs8vfocc?t=900)).

These positions are less opposed than they look. Moromisato and Perry are talking about breadth of distinct experiences that a run can surface ([George Moromisato 2016, 8:42](https://youtu.be/QBZkvtGucBU?t=522); [Jon Perry 2025, 7:14](https://youtu.be/NlxGPKV0PrY?t=434)); Dias, Wehrle and Wilson are warning about volume that is cheap, unintended or padded ([Bruno Dias 2016, 11:49](https://youtu.be/UGPkEWqwSAY?t=709); [Cole Wehrle 2025, 19:31](https://youtu.be/HgnvMBVKP0M?t=1171); [Rich Wilson 2021, 11:22](https://youtu.be/wtlLa7BGZcs?t=682)). What the choice depends on is whether each additional piece of content gives the player something they can recognise and care about, which is the subject of the next section. Wehrle's small persistent deck and NetHack's sprawl suit different relationships between player and content.

### A usable standard

If "infinite" is the wrong goal, what is the right one? Jeff Emtman and Martin Austwick give a modest, workable bar for Neutrinowatch, their self-generating podcast: it need not be infinitely procedural, but one listen should not be boring, and a second listen should give you something a little different ([Jeff Emtman and Martin Austwick 2024, 20:54](https://youtu.be/1sZlIfCcz_c?t=1254)). Apply the same test to your content: is it enjoyable the first time a player meets it, and does it offer something new the second time?

## The oatmeal problem: making difference perceptible

### Difference the player cannot see does not exist

Kate Compton's image of "10,000 bowls of oatmeal" recurs across these talks: you can generate countless mathematically unique bowls, but the player sees a lot of oatmeal. Max Kreminski relays it as a point about perception: if players cannot see differences that are meaningful to them, they stop seeing differences at all, so a large number of possibilities is not enough to keep them invested ([Max Kreminski 2018, 14:36](https://youtu.be/TvlZinAvpwg?t=876)). Bruno Dias and Liza Knipscher both build their approaches around the same problem ([Bruno Dias 2016, 9:58](https://youtu.be/UGPkEWqwSAY?t=598); [Liza Knipscher 2025, 21:02](https://youtu.be/jBhcHdV5HHo?t=1262)). Florence Smith Nicholls notes that reality TV faces it too, under the name of conceptual uniqueness: a format must keep generating interesting content, and limited diversity of characters, a criticism made of Love Island and also of Hades, makes it feel boring ([Florence Smith Nicholls 2023, 10:10](https://youtu.be/MQw3pe-z6JM?t=610)).

### Independent attributes make every place the same

Alex Byaly identifies a structural cause. If you generate each attribute independently from fixed weights, for example drawing each character's city, species, food, job and crime from its own weighted raffle, then every subset of the population looks exactly like the whole. Filter to one city and the numbers shrink, but every proportion stays the same; he calls this perfectly symmetrical data, and bad ([Alex Byaly 2022, 4:24](https://youtu.be/otEv5dh2f4E?t=264)). The consequence for play is direct: once you have met everyone in one town and learned its species and job mix, the next town is the same, so there is no reason to go ([Alex Byaly 2022, 6:12](https://youtu.be/otEv5dh2f4E?t=372)).

His remedy is to reproduce the arbitrary local correlations of the real world, where answers to a survey vary by restaurant, time of day and city for no obvious reason, and where people act differently when you travel; those coincidences are part of what makes exploring fun ([Alex Byaly 2022, 5:29](https://youtu.be/otEv5dh2f4E?t=329)). He points to two games that do this. Tales of Maj'Eyal generates item properties in bundles called egos, so "of clarity" brings mental save and confusion immunity together, and which egos are available depends on item type (rings and shoes have different lists); knowing one stat tells you something about others ([Alex Byaly 2022, 7:09](https://youtu.be/otEv5dh2f4E?t=429)). Dwarf Fortress gets patterns by reproducing real-world models such as erosion and biomes, and by running a strategy-game simulation during history generation, where some actors win and others lose and leave patterned results even from unpatterned starts ([Alex Byaly 2022, 9:53](https://youtu.be/otEv5dh2f4E?t=593)).

### Vary the higher-level structure

Several talks converge on the same move: correlate or bundle variation at a level above individual attributes. Jason Grinblat ties Caves of Qud's history generator explicitly to the oatmeal problem and answers it with macro variation in the structure of society: a high succession rate can produce a dynasty (one history had four of five sultans from one family), and a city's locations may be organised by wealth (palaces, slums, middle-class districts) or by function (garrison quarter, museum quarter, hippodrome) ([Jason Grinblat 2017, 22:11](https://youtu.be/ClGAApZYIvI?t=1331)). Darius Kazemi describes Emily Short's generated travel guide, which is openly templated (each chapter a county with a tavern, geography and a castle) but stays interesting because each town gets one of a few distinct aesthetic "elements", fertile and fungal versus prim and proper, instead of a soup of every trait ([Darius Kazemi 2017, 28:11](https://youtu.be/CLi4PWxDmAI?t=1691)).

Knipscher shows the same principle on creatures. Two genetically very different rabbits in Bioloom still look like rabbits, so she pushes the axes players can see: grouping species into herds made four similar species read as distinct, a tiny rat beside a large dinosaur feels different, and a radially symmetrical eight-legged creature is hard to confuse with a torso-head-legs animal even in the same colour ([Liza Knipscher 2025, 21:02](https://youtu.be/jBhcHdV5HHo?t=1262)).

### Text as a cheap source of difference

Dias offers another lever. In Voyageur, text acts as a lens on the world model that picks a different angle each time: there are roughly ten thousand combinations of the six most important planetary factors, but a city world may read as a foreboding, rainy gothic metropolis or as a utopia depending on the prose ([Bruno Dias 2016, 9:34](https://youtu.be/UGPkEWqwSAY?t=574)). Text is good at perceptual difference because it is expressive and easy to recombine, and small background generators add detail cheaply; Voyageur's fusion-food generator draws on a simple word list yet produces things like "salted stuffed octopus fritters" that paint a planet's culture ([Bruno Dias 2016, 9:58](https://youtu.be/UGPkEWqwSAY?t=598)). His goal is not endless longevity but a universe of digestible glimpses where each planet has a detail you have not seen.

### In practice

- **Correlate attributes.** Generate bundles (Maj'Eyal's egos) or run a process whose winners and losers leave patterns (Dwarf Fortress) rather than drawing each property independently ([Alex Byaly 2022, 7:09](https://youtu.be/otEv5dh2f4E?t=429); [Alex Byaly 2022, 9:53](https://youtu.be/otEv5dh2f4E?t=593)).
- **Vary at the macro level.** Give each region, society or town one organising idea that colours everything in it ([Jason Grinblat 2017, 22:11](https://youtu.be/ClGAApZYIvI?t=1331); [Darius Kazemi 2017, 28:11](https://youtu.be/CLi4PWxDmAI?t=1691)).
- **Exaggerate the visible axes.** Scale, silhouette and grouping are what players perceive first ([Liza Knipscher 2025, 21:02](https://youtu.be/jBhcHdV5HHo?t=1262)).
- **Vary repeated pieces cosmetically.** Sergio Garces varies each placed prefab internally, with rotation and offset where allowed, alternative models, colour and open or closed doors, so one car prefab placed six times becomes a small car, a sedan and a pickup in different colours; the techniques stack ([Sergio Garces 2022, 20:54](https://youtu.be/6U8c6hbVJLY?t=1254)).
- **Make differences matter mechanically.** Isaac Karth notes that Dwarf Fortress's Forgotten Beasts are only short descriptions, yet are memorable and have inspired reams of fan art because their properties change what happens to your fortress: it matters whether a beast is made of bronze or water, because one kills far more dwarves ([Isaac Karth 2019, 4:39](https://youtu.be/MHEkE7nPuZc?t=279)).

> It matters if it is made out of bronze or water. One of those is going to kill a lot more of my dwarfs. — [Isaac Karth 2019, 4:39](https://youtu.be/MHEkE7nPuZc?t=279)

## Baselines, spikes and rarity: shaping the distribution

### Plain backgrounds make the strange stand out

How memorable generated output is depends on the shape of its distribution, not only on its size. Two talks from different domains reach the same conclusion. Cat Manning, drawing on Emily Short, describes the "venom" principle: a few spiky, statistically unlikely characters or traits should stand out against a mostly unremarkable cast. Crusader Kings II does not need every character to be interesting, only enough standouts to pick from among hundreds; if everyone had a rich backstory it would overwhelm. The ratio scales with how many characters the player deals with, so in a game with only five, two or three interesting ones will not do ([Cat Manning 2020, 16:20](https://youtu.be/q7E1N-fJnrA?t=980)). Elliot Trinidad hit the same wall with Blaseball's name generator. After seasons of bombastic user-submitted names, the narrative team asked for plenty of plain "just some guy" names, because when every name is special none of them is ([Elliot Trinidad 2023, 11:45](https://youtu.be/9yFferxbrBU?t=705)).

> When they're all special none of them are that special. You kind of need the more plain names in that field to make the other ones shine. — [Elliot Trinidad 2023, 11:45](https://youtu.be/9yFferxbrBU?t=705)

### Rarity tiers and rare exceptions

The technique that follows from this is to build an explicit rare tail. Joe Sondow's Emoji Aquarium bot uses tiers: fish and plants every three hours, occasionally a squid or crab, and every few days super-rare junk such as dice or a game controller. When followers ask for more squid he refuses, because the scarcity is what makes it a prize ([Joe Sondow 2017, 3:54](https://youtu.be/4byHHDeVKoA?t=234)). Jon Perry builds Mini and Max's microscopic levels from "atoms" classed as common, uncommon and rare, like Magic cards, so rare atoms extend the tail of novelty after the common ones are familiar; extra logic spaces out key items so the content budget is not spent at once ([Jon Perry 2025, 16:06](https://youtu.be/NlxGPKV0PrY?t=966)).

Percentage-gated features give the same effect within a single kind of output. Jason Grinblat, citing Compton's idea of "characterfulness" (being perceived by a human as meaningfully different, not merely technically different), gives Caves of Qud's generated books occasional distinctive features: an author's or editor's note 10% of the time, a tome ten times normal size 5% of the time, and a title modifier such as "Nth edition" 20% of the time ([Jason Grinblat 2016, 16:44](https://youtu.be/zDTQM0Ipiz4?t=1004)). Knipscher gives almost every socket in Bioloom a small chance to spawn almost any body part, which yields a creature with a giant hand for a nose or a grub with horse heads for legs ([Liza Knipscher 2025, 8:32](https://youtu.be/jBhcHdV5HHo?t=512)). Ada Null's Kiss Garden adds subtle variants (hookups, friends-with-benefits and romances each shift the prose slightly) and rare surreal passages where the narrator obsesses over a plant and strings phrases together with random conjunctions; she calls these a "rare special tree", a pointed moment of uniqueness in a sea of sameness ([Ada Null 2025, 9:24](https://youtu.be/VzoruhRyvqQ?t=564)).

Rare misfits also keep a pool from feeling solved. About one in eight calls in Paris Buttfield-Addison's Hintline 93 is a wrong number, someone wanting pizza or describing the wrong console, and he suggests roguelikes do the same with, for example, a room that does not fit the rest of the floor ([Paris Buttfield-Addison 2026, 6:31:27](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=23487)).

### With or without replacement

Whether you draw with replacement changes what the player experiences. Paul Dean describes Pacific Drive's fax machine as working like a deck of cards, giving one unique strange story or message per use as a collectible reward for players who explore off the beaten path ([Paul Dean 2025, 12:27](https://youtu.be/nLqLOzrjkYU?t=747)). Evan Debenham uses decks for a different purpose in Shattered Pixel Dungeon: regular items still use weighting, but loot rooms draw from two shuffled decks interwoven together, with drawn cards returned rather than reshuffling and an occasional second or third draw for unpredictability. The aim is consistency across a run, avoiding cases like an early player finding four of the same armour type when only the first is useful ([Evan Debenham 2022, 8:10](https://youtu.be/kaojiu9syPE?t=490)).

Set that against John Harris's account of the Mystery Dungeon games. Many of them weight generation so powerful items appear only deeper, but the first Shiren lets great items turn up early, which can transform a run, much as in NetHack, and Harris counts this as one of the best reasons to play it ([John Harris 2024, 14:18](https://youtu.be/0MdNwIHwXy0?t=858)). Debenham's decks smooth out the swings; Shiren keeps them as a source of run-defining stories. Which you want depends on whether your game's variety comes mainly from steady build decisions or from adapting to rare windfalls.

### Placement rules

The distribution also has a spatial and temporal side.

- **An empty entry.** Xalavier Nelson Jr.'s An Airport for Aliens Currently Run by Dogs includes "emptystrians" in its pedestrian list: picking one spawns nothing, which gives a basic simulation of crowd flow, such as a near-empty airport early in the morning ([Xalavier Nelson Jr. 2020, 8:36](https://youtu.be/SjttI9N9KSM?t=516)).
- **A one-line rule.** Darius Kazemi cites Spelunky's treasure rule: the chance of treasure on a tile is proportional to the number of walls around it, so open floor rarely has loot, a nook bounded on three sides probably does, and an empty pocket inside rock very likely does ([Darius Kazemi 2017, 15:46](https://youtu.be/CLi4PWxDmAI?t=946)).
- **A special case.** Spelunky also has inelegant rules, such as at most one giant spider per cave level, placed under a brick with a 2x2 empty space below, outside shops and start rooms, at a 1-in-40 chance ([Darius Kazemi 2017, 16:59](https://youtu.be/CLi4PWxDmAI?t=1019)). Both kinds of rule have their place.
- **Dropping constraints on purpose.** Alexei Pepers describes Caves of Qud's Six Day Stilt, a pilgrimage site where creatures are peaceful, so it drops both difficulty and biome constraints and lets early players glimpse late-game creatures and wonder how to fight them; merchants similarly sell high-level recipes early because they are useless without late materials ([Alexei Pepers 2025, 42:31](https://youtu.be/H5EU9_Gdu94?t=2551)).
- **Odds that depend on state.** In NetHack, a wish for a named artifact is likelier to fail the more artifacts already exist in the game, so the speedrunner Adeon checks for randomly spawned artifacts before wishing ([Adeon 2017, 59:26](https://youtu.be/rIB0y_kwFuY?t=3566)).

### In practice

Choose a baseline that is deliberately plain, then add a rare tail with explicit percentages or tiers, and tune the ratio to how many items the player will actually look at ([Cat Manning 2020, 16:20](https://youtu.be/q7E1N-fJnrA?t=980); [Elliot Trinidad 2023, 11:45](https://youtu.be/9yFferxbrBU?t=705)). Decide for each pool whether it should draw without replacement (unique stories, consistent loot) or with replacement (the chance of repeats and early windfalls), and resist players' requests to make the rare thing common ([Joe Sondow 2017, 3:54](https://youtu.be/4byHHDeVKoA?t=234)).

## Constraint, theme and intention

### A smaller space can be a better one

The instinct with generative systems is to want more. Aaron A. Reed argues that limiting the generative space can be more powerful than expanding it, because it lets every output meet a higher authored standard while still feeling unique ([Aaron A. Reed 2020, 12:39](https://youtu.be/x0Xh4oCX9t0?t=759)). For his novel Subcutanean he trimmed scene variations into a cozier, curated space focused on changes that say something meaningful about the characters. Each print-on-demand order generates a new version from a seed tracked in a database; Reed avoided GPT-style generation and hand-sculpted variation in secrets, revelations, character beats and resolutions, and reviewers say they cannot imagine the story happening any other way ([Aaron A. Reed 2020, 14:47](https://youtu.be/x0Xh4oCX9t0?t=887)).

Cole Wehrle makes the converse warning: too much obfuscation turns procedural content into white noise, as in early procedurally generated first-person games like Daggerfall whose worlds felt empty and foggy. The goal is content with intention that makes players feel they are in a lived world, and as a tabletop designer he often hand-designs each of, say, ten magic swords rather than generating them ([Cole Wehrle 2025, 10:21](https://youtu.be/HgnvMBVKP0M?t=621)).

> We aren't just trying to generate content but content with intention. — [Cole Wehrle 2025, 10:21](https://youtu.be/HgnvMBVKP0M?t=621)

### Theme is the glue

What lets recombined pieces cohere is a shared theme. Matt Carney points to Shadows of Doubt, which recombines many detailed handwritten elements that can be recombined because all of them sit under the umbrella of noir ([Matt Carney 2026, 20:18](https://youtu.be/SU-VcmsOvZo?t=1218)). He contrasts Caves of Qud, whose possibility space is very wide and welcomes dissonance, allowing generation unless it feels extremely off, but which also has narrow, targeted generation such as sultan shrines themed around elements like ice or fire ([Matt Carney 2026, 20:27](https://youtu.be/SU-VcmsOvZo?t=1227)). Bruno Dias keeps Voyageur's planets consistent with a symbolic system of six ideological and aesthetic alignments that permeate the content ([Bruno Dias 2016, 8:37](https://youtu.be/UGPkEWqwSAY?t=517)).

Theme also generates content in the first place. Alice Lai describes how Hades uses mythology as a generator for art and mechanics in parallel: thinking about what Zeus grants spins up both, and when the call system was added, Zeus got abilities reflecting his vengeful character, a self-feeding "water wheel" of content ([Alice Lai 2021, 17:44](https://youtu.be/pXib0WTfLbI?t=1064)). And theme is a filter. Jim Shepard writes Dungeonmans' monsters like field-guide entries for real beasts, one notch above standard fantasy, with an ecology even when they are funny; cartoonish monsters such as smiling slimes and a proposed boss called Clownicus were cut because they did not fit ([Jim Shepard 2016, 13:11](https://youtu.be/_Si626-Y_q0?t=791)). Joe Sondow applies the same discipline to scale and viewpoint: Emoji Aquarium works because emoji are drawn from the side, and he admits only rare swimmers whose size fits, so dolphins and sharks are in and whales are out ([Joe Sondow 2017, 3:05](https://youtu.be/4byHHDeVKoA?t=185)).

Numbers carry tone too. Ben Berman observes that small, single-digit stats feel designed, as in Hearthstone, where players sense a human considered each card, while precise multi-digit numbers like Clash Royale's feel triangulated and over-tuned ([Ben Berman 2017, 17:05](https://youtu.be/Z6lHExfem6U?t=1025)). If generated stats should feel authored, keep them small.

### Exposure versus obscurity

Wehrle offers two observations that pull against each other. Random tables show the whole generative space transparently, which he loves (roll two d12s for an NPC ailment, and the whole space fits on a screen), but the more players understand how generation works, the more it undoes itself; by the third lovesick turtle they see the adjectives propping up the story ([Cole Wehrle 2025, 8:47](https://youtu.be/HgnvMBVKP0M?t=527)). Tales of the Arabian Nights, by contrast, makes a simple choose-your-own-adventure structure feel like an open world by layering obscuring steps between choice and outcome: draw an encounter card, consult a matrix, look up the result in a binder, like riding a train through a foggy switchyard ([Cole Wehrle 2025, 9:35](https://youtu.be/HgnvMBVKP0M?t=575)). Yet he also warns that too much obfuscation becomes white noise ([Cole Wehrle 2025, 10:21](https://youtu.be/HgnvMBVKP0M?t=621)). The balance he points to is enough indirection that the machinery is not visible, with enough intention behind each outcome that it still means something.

### Mixing curated and generated material

Not everything should be generated. A speaker at the 2018 lightning talks puts all generated content on a familiarity continuum: the less familiar the audience is with the real thing, the easier it is to generate convincingly. Alien spacecraft are easy, human faces are hardest, and you should never procedurally generate a '57 Chevy; this is why he generated extraterrestrial whales in alien seas ([Various 2018, 37:40](https://youtu.be/60MTG-__dt4?t=2260)).

Curation also comes in degrees. Florence Smith Nicholls notes that Love Island's generated content is heavily edited, with a spin-off show for material interesting enough to air but not canonical, and compares this to Bad News, where James Ryan curated in real time how an actor responded to a participant ([Florence Smith Nicholls 2023, 3:57](https://youtu.be/MQw3pe-z6JM?t=237)). And static content gives players a common thread. Tyler Coleman relays that Caves of Qud's fans talk roughly half about its static characters and things, such as spine fruit always leading to spine fruit jam, and half about what its generative systems produce ([Tyler Coleman 2024, 23:25](https://youtu.be/C6jR41fZjqM?t=1405)). Hand-authored fixed points and generated variety serve different parts of the community's conversation.

## Authoring content to combine: parts, tags, variants and possibility spaces

### Decide what the output is for, then generate mechanics first

A generator's design starts from the question of what output makes play interesting, not from modelling existing rules. Atty Vohra, building a monster generator for D&D 5e, found it easy to model Monster Manual stat blocks; the real design question was what kinds of output lead to interesting combat encounters ([Atty Vohra 2021, 3:54](https://youtu.be/0ydWz1EvMJs?t=234)). His answer inverts the usual order: the generator produces numbers and mechanics first, and the human designer invents a monster and fiction that justify them, which he finds easier and faster ([Atty Vohra 2021, 4:43](https://youtu.be/0ydWz1EvMJs?t=283)). He describes the mechanics as abstract adjective-verb pairs within a limited mechanical subspace, such as "drain resource", where "drain" might mean hit points or spell slots. Faced with a drain/gain pattern, necromancy spells, 45 movement speed, high charisma and a paradoxical resistance and vulnerability to piercing, he invented a haunted princess ghost who drains spell slots to flicker between planes, which explains the paradox ([Atty Vohra 2021, 5:31](https://youtu.be/0ydWz1EvMJs?t=331)). The abstraction is the point: it constrains and inspires the human rather than dictating to them.

### Build an explicit possibility space

Jasper Cole and Leigh Alexander converge on a related practice: build an explicit matrix of categories and mine it. Cole says Backpack Hero had to be recoded because its original item system was not flexible enough, and advises building a wide, flexible possibility space for items early and then exploring it fully, so you and modders can create varied loot that makes players interact with the game in new ways ([Jasper Cole 2023, 27:35](https://youtu.be/COeJTtSDd78?t=1655)). His items are built from three lists:

- **Triggers:** on use, each turn, turn end, once per combat, on enemy defeat.
- **Effects:** damage, block, heal, energy, max health.
- **Targets:** player, one enemy, all enemies, everyone.

With that matrix you can look for combinations not yet used and design an item with no idea going in. Given a rose sprite with no function, Cole reasoned that a rose is not something you use, so chose a start-of-turn trigger and then fitting effect and target ([Jasper Cole 2023, 17:06](https://youtu.be/COeJTtSDd78?t=1026)). The matrix is one source among several; Backpack Hero items also come from known needs (the wooden sword as simplest starter), Discord contests, grid shapes ("what about an L-shaped item?"), seasonal sets, and an artist's sheet of 100 drawings worked backwards into mechanics ([Jasper Cole 2023, 13:55](https://youtu.be/COeJTtSDd78?t=835)).

Alexander, writing hundreds of lines for McMansion, gave each celebrity two Pokémon elemental types (Steve Harvey as poison/grass) and wrote behaviours per element, which she found much easier than writing from a blank page ([Leigh Alexander 2023, 24:24](https://youtu.be/NjYS8XmeaiY?t=1464)). She chose the Pokémon table because its affinities and oppositions suited a game about relationships, and advises borrowing how other games organise information and translating your content into that structure ([Leigh Alexander 2023, 35:30](https://youtu.be/NjYS8XmeaiY?t=2130)). She also recommends fixing the organisational matrix before writing, even arbitrarily, so content types are evenly distributed and tag coverage is assured; in McMansion each element needs a quote, a question, two- and three-person interactions, and positive and negative variants, and she hand-tweaked every line, which she credits for how well generated combinations fit together ([Leigh Alexander 2023, 28:40](https://youtu.be/NjYS8XmeaiY?t=1720)). Ezra Szanton adds that changing what surrounds a fixed pool, through card packs, per-character card sets or rule changes, lets players learn a new synergy network from the same cards, citing Star Vaders, Super Auto Pets, Party House, Slay the Spire and Dicey Dungeons ([Ezra Szanton 2025, 24:19](https://youtu.be/JfNeYtH7xI4?t=1459)).

### Data patterns that multiply content

The authoring format decides how much content gets written. Kate Compton says that if she had had to write an if statement for each patron description, she would not have written so much text; Tracery, the text-grammar tool her talk presents (described further under assembled text below), exists so that writing a lot of content is painless ([Kate Compton 2016, 10:15](https://youtu.be/isB82kORimk?t=615)).

Patrick Kemp describes the config patterns Spry Fox built up over years, concrete enough to copy:

- **Tag references.** Loot tables, crafting recipes and shop inventories reference items by tag rather than by ID, with tags in a central registry. A designer makes a new item, assigns tags, and it flows into every relevant system without anyone maintaining item lists ([Patrick Kemp 2023, 5:57](https://youtu.be/rWPJ5fW1UH8?t=357)).
- **Variants.** Fields wrapped in chevrons in a config are marked for substitution, and the system generates one item for every combination of the variant arrays. With arrays for type, season and rarity, one flower config yields 3 x 4 x 3 = 36 flowers in the simplified example; variants can change colour, icon, sprite or economic behaviour, and Cozy Grove's hundreds of collectible flowers come largely from one config ([Patrick Kemp 2023, 10:12](https://youtu.be/rWPJ5fW1UH8?t=612)).
- **Mods.** Within a variant, mods adjust numeric properties of the base config, so an uncommon rarity variant can change drop weight and buy and sell prices. Shared variants such as rarity live in a global file, so mushrooms, flowers or fish simply include them ([Patrick Kemp 2023, 11:18](https://youtu.be/rWPJ5fW1UH8?t=678)).

The payoff is expansibility: adding a new season or species is a few lines that multiply into all their variations, and the tag substrate creates emergent connections ([Patrick Kemp 2023, 12:56](https://youtu.be/rWPJ5fW1UH8?t=776)).

Tags can also carry meaning between generators. Pierre Vigier's room generator receives a context of tags from a higher-level generator, and room descriptions include objects that appear only if their trigger tag is present, such as a telescope for a character who loves astronomy; this keeps generators loosely coupled while letting rooms say something about the world ([Pierre Vigier 2022, 13:07](https://youtu.be/oVhq8V93gHM?t=787)).

Thomas Robertson's procedural super attacks show the same separation of concerns for functional content. His architecture is a trio: a dictionary that generates the list of available attacks (like a Pokémon move chart or spell book), a choreographer that scripts each attack from atoms, and a director that plays the script. The director knows every atom and can inform the dictionary, so attacks are defined around the "middle" atoms that travel between source and target; in practice choreographing became a function on the director ([Thomas Robertson 2021, 5:53](https://youtu.be/f1t4yPjfZyM?t=353)). Each attack record stores a name, colour, tags, level and random seed, so handing the record to the choreographer always regenerates the same attack. In his test bed the dictionary built five attacks at levels one to five for each of three middle atoms, 15 in all, and string tags let code ask for "the middle ones" or "the red ones" ([Thomas Robertson 2021, 10:03](https://youtu.be/f1t4yPjfZyM?t=603)). Spencer Egart notes that the node-based, step-by-step tooling used for dungeon geometry can equally place encounters and loot or generate items, for example by piping through base-item and curse nodes ([Spencer Egart 2021, 8:35](https://youtu.be/YfLYPIXGF7E?t=515)).

### Assembling from modular parts

The simplest assembly pattern is a chain of picks. Xalavier Nelson Jr.'s airport pedestrians pick a character type from a list, and that object picks a line and a visual from two more lists, producing, for instance, a super-buff dog thinking of his parents' sacrifices while lifting weights ([Xalavier Nelson Jr. 2020, 8:57](https://youtu.be/SjttI9N9KSM?t=537)).

Visual and physical assembly needs more structure. Knipscher builds Bioloom's creatures from body-part prefabs kept deliberately simple so they combine in stranger ways, with tiling textures and a shader that lerps between two tints defined in the creature's genes ([Liza Knipscher 2025, 6:32](https://youtu.be/jBhcHdV5HHo?t=392)). Each prefab has empty child objects called sockets marking where another part can attach, each with its own spawn odds; sockets sharing a manually assigned ID spawn the same part, giving symmetric eyes, wings or legs, and the odds make a torso likely to get a head at the front, a tail at the back, legs at the sides and horns along the spine ([Liza Knipscher 2025, 7:42](https://youtu.be/jBhcHdV5HHo?t=462)). Generation proceeds layer by layer until sockets run out or a limit is hit, and past about four layers results get less interesting ([Liza Knipscher 2025, 8:32](https://youtu.be/jBhcHdV5HHo?t=512)).

Breeding exposed a pitfall. Naively combining random parts from each parent's chromosome produced broken creatures: a horn where the neck should be left no socket for head and eyes, giving, for example, a shrub with one leg that rolled around until it died. Offspring are now regenerated from the prefab probabilities, constrained to parts present in the parents, which looks good but loses placement, so a horse-head leg passes on as a part but not as a leg ([Liza Knipscher 2025, 13:49](https://youtu.be/jBhcHdV5HHo?t=829)). Gabriel Koenig avoided that class of failure in Test Tube Titans by mutating a working physics-based bipedal template: changing limb weights and shapes produced characters that move and handle differently, some more agile and some worse, but all functional ([Gabriel Koenig 2020, 8:49](https://youtu.be/xju91VGh2Ps?t=529)). The lesson both cases point to is to vary around something known to work, or to constrain recombination by the structure that makes a part valid.

Constraints also make visual output cohere. Younès Rabii's Tea Garden generates flowers from a 6x6 pixel grid, applies a symmetry (horizontal, diagonal and so on), and colours it with at most two colours from the PICO-8 palette, whose colours already match, so results are strange but sometimes compelling ([Younès Rabii 2020, 2:54](https://youtu.be/s6Kxh_Zyiqs?t=174)). Sea of Rifts builds ships and buildings from modular kit pieces assembled in-engine; Sofie Kjær Schmidt notes that about three roof types serve ten ship types, and anyone on the team can assemble a ship ([Alexander Birke and Sofie Kjær Schmidt 2025, 15:57](https://youtu.be/FC9GAL2piJI?t=957)). For the sunken city, Alexander Birke wrote a simple generator that stacks modules vertically under rules (repeat one, two, three, or random) and then left artists to use it freely, and they found uses he had not planned, such as extending pillars down from a top section ([Alexander Birke and Sofie Kjær Schmidt 2025, 22:07](https://youtu.be/FC9GAL2piJI?t=1327)).

### Functional content is the hard frontier

Generating things that must play well is harder than generating things that must look varied. Ben Berman calls functional content, such as monster behaviours or playable cards, the next frontier beyond level layouts, observing that a Hearthstone card is really a roguelike monster in disguise ([Ben Berman 2017, 29:29](https://youtu.be/Z6lHExfem6U?t=1769)). He also warns that a strategy card must both look good and play good, since nobody picks a card that looks bad even if it plays well; Slay the Spire tested by showing people three cards and seeing which they chose, and he suggests cutting anything that fails either test and perhaps feeding pick data back into generation ([Benjamin Berman 2019, 19:45](https://youtu.be/DT9_7sW5knY?t=1185)).

## Names, languages and speech

The principles so far (perceptible difference, a shaped distribution, theme, authoring for combination) apply to every kind of content. The rest of the chapter takes the kinds one at a time, starting with the smallest unit that still carries a world: the name.

A name generator that only produces variety is wasting most of what names can do. Names tell the player where someone comes from, which people belong together and which are strangers, and what kind of world this is ([Sraëka-Lillian 2021, 1:37](https://youtu.be/XQKNwaCwD-I?t=97); [Elliot Trinidad 2023, 21:31](https://youtu.be/9yFferxbrBU?t=1291)). The talks that treat names seriously design the generator for identity first and variety second.

### One generator per culture

Sraëka-Lillian's starting point is that names recognisably drawn from the same language tie characters to a culture. If your game generates arbitrarily many worlds and cultures, a single name generator cannot do that job: you need to generate the name generators themselves, one per culture ([Sraëka-Lillian 2021, 1:37](https://youtu.be/XQKNwaCwD-I?t=97)). She gives three tests for the output. It should be varied (a few similar names are fine, as English has John, June and Jan, but most should differ), internally cohesive (recurring sound patterns across many names, as in Latin masculine names) and externally distinctive (Japanese names do not look like Latin ones) ([Sraëka-Lillian 2021, 4:05](https://youtu.be/XQKNwaCwD-I?t=245)).

> A language that is both internally cohesive and externally distinctive is likely to have a strong sense of identity. — [Sraëka-Lillian 2021, 4:05](https://youtu.be/XQKNwaCwD-I?t=245)

Mark R Johnson pursues the same goal in Ultima Ratio Regum. Each culture gets a set of letters clumped into syllables, and every proper noun that culture produces (people, surnames, nicknames, towns, cities, artworks) is built from those pieces, so a row of names from one culture looks alike and differs from its neighbours ([Mark R Johnson 2019, 12:53](https://youtu.be/qh9vyoMviJI?t=773)). On top of the sounds he generates the *shape* of names: at world creation, dozens of name-style pieces are stitched into pairs or triplets to form each culture's naming archetype, from Homeric-epithet-like styles to ones no real language uses. The archetypes are reassigned every world, and a player can learn to guess an NPC's culture from the style of their name alone ([Mark R Johnson 2019, 17:09](https://youtu.be/qh9vyoMviJI?t=1029)).

### The phonology toolkit

Sraëka-Lillian's talk is specific enough to build from. The steps, in order:

- **A small master inventory.** Over 2,000 sounds exist across human languages, but keep the inventory small and mostly to sounds your players already know how to pronounce. Avoid diacritics, which read as visual noise to English readers, and add a few common non-English sounds that are spelled close to how they sound, for flavour ([Sraëka-Lillian 2021, 7:29](https://youtu.be/XQKNwaCwD-I?t=449)).
- **Per-language sound sets weighted by prevalence.** Choose each language's phonemes independently, weighted by how common each sound is across real languages (cross-language databases online give the figures). Correlated selection might be more cohesive, but in practice the difference is subtle, so independent selection is fine ([Sraëka-Lillian 2021, 9:03](https://youtu.be/XQKNwaCwD-I?t=543)).
- **Phonotactics.** The rules for how sounds combine shape the output more than the inventory does: syllable structure (onset, nucleus, coda, and whether onsets and codas may hold several consonants), positional frequency (English *h* starts syllables but never ends them) and limits on which consonants may touch. Without those limits you get "consonant soup" ([Sraëka-Lillian 2021, 10:42](https://youtu.be/XQKNwaCwD-I?t=642)).
- **Recurring morphemes.** Reusing meaningful chunks across names signals intentional structure. When two morphemes meet and the sounds clash, the cheapest fix is the one real languages use most: delete one of the offending sounds ([Sraëka-Lillian 2021, 11:48](https://youtu.be/XQKNwaCwD-I?t=708)).

Behind all of these sits pronounceability. A name a player can find no way to say is hard to remember and decays into noise; the pronunciation they settle on need not be "correct", but there has to be one ([Sraëka-Lillian 2021, 4:41](https://youtu.be/XQKNwaCwD-I?t=281)). When a generated name still looks wrong, you have two honest options: change the strategy or add a safeguard, or embrace the weirdness. Sraëka-Lillian urges humility before reaching for the fix, since an English speaker's sense of "normal" comes from a handful of European and Asian languages, and a name that looks broken may be ordinary in a language you do not know ([Sraëka-Lillian 2021, 12:27](https://youtu.be/XQKNwaCwD-I?t=747)).

### The deliberately simple alternative

Blaseball shows the other end of the scale. Elliot Trinidad describes a generator that picks a random first name and a random last name, with no repeat checks and no alliteration weighting; tuning it meant curating the lists, not writing code, which let the community design team work while the programmers were busy. Trinidad says his talk is really about thoughtful manual curation rather than procedural generation ([Elliot Trinidad 2023, 8:24](https://youtu.be/9yFferxbrBU?t=504)). Several of his curation rules are portable:

- **No tiers.** Dozens of generated characters appear together, so every one is treated equally: cool-sounding names are not saved for bosses or elites, and the tone is the dry humour of real pro sports rather than a wink at the player ([Elliot Trinidad 2023, 6:10](https://youtu.be/9yFferxbrBU?t=370)). This works alongside the plain "just some guy" names described under baselines and spikes: the strange names stand out because they are mixed in with ordinary ones, not because they are reserved for important characters.
- **Themed cycles.** Adding names around recurring themes (animals, foods), like the card cycles in Magic: The Gathering, gives a random pool internal consistency and lets players group names instead of facing hundreds of unrelated ones; the patterns also imply how parents in the world name their children ([Elliot Trinidad 2023, 21:31](https://youtu.be/9yFferxbrBU?t=1291)).
- **Careful sourcing.** When drawing real names from cultures you do not know, cross-reference many sources such as census data rather than trusting a single baby-name site, and research how the names are transcribed into English ([Elliot Trinidad 2023, 19:23](https://youtu.be/9yFferxbrBU?t=1163)).

The two approaches are not as far apart as they look. Both aim for names that say something about the world; Sraëka-Lillian and Johnson get there by generating the rules of a language, Trinidad by curating real-world lists into themes ([Sraëka-Lillian 2021, 4:05](https://youtu.be/XQKNwaCwD-I?t=245); [Elliot Trinidad 2023, 21:31](https://youtu.be/9yFferxbrBU?t=1291)). The choice depends on whether your cultures are invented per world (then you need generated phonology) or fixed (then curated lists may be all you need).

### Place names

Places need the same thinking. Jim Shepard describes how Dungeonmans uses a different naming scheme per location type so players get the right feeling about a place without remembering its name: regular dungeons include the names of about 30 legendary past figures to say that greatness happened there, while bandit camps, lizardman caves and roadblocks named like battles each have their own style ([Jim Shepard 2016, 16:06](https://youtu.be/_Si626-Y_q0?t=966)). His warning is that invented words have to mean something. Shepard got lost among Lord of the Rings Online's Tolkien-derived names, so Dungeonmans' special towers mix one strange word with understandable ones ("Tower Unparalleled"), enough to suggest that an unknown historical people built them ([Jim Shepard 2016, 16:26](https://youtu.be/_Si626-Y_q0?t=986)).

### Speech

Once cultures have names, it is tempting to give them languages. Johnson considered a learnable in-game language for a long time and found it collapses into the Final Fantasy X model, a substitution cipher for English. Ultima Ratio Regum instead treats English as a trade language that every culture speaks in its own dialect and manner ([Mark R Johnson 2019, 12:10](https://youtu.be/qh9vyoMviJI?t=730)). The culture shows in *what* is said: greetings, farewells, compliments and insults are generated from what each culture prizes and despises and vary with the speaker's opinion of the player, so a culture that respects only artistic skill will not compliment you for wit ([Mark R Johnson 2019, 20:12](https://youtu.be/qh9vyoMviJI?t=1212)). It also shows in how much is said. The same "welcome to our country" ranges from brusque to lengthy depending on cultural verbosity, the speaker's personality and their inclination toward the player, which changes how useful asking around actually is ([Mark R Johnson 2019, 21:44](https://youtu.be/qh9vyoMviJI?t=1304)).

### Names alone make players care

The cheapest evidence that names matter comes from Kingdom of Loathing. Zack Johnson describes randomly naming the identical trash mobs in the hobo raid dungeon, starting from John Hodgman's 700 hobo names (used with permission) split up and extended with names reflecting traits like hot elemental attacks, so that repetitive fights felt less grindy. Players shared screenshots of hobos named after their friends, and the response to the generated names was often better than to hand-written content, which Johnson found "kind of demoralizing" ([Zack Johnson 2016, 8:41](https://youtu.be/jNUMRG_tvrY?t=521)). Nick Cummings points out that real baseball shows the same effect: its history is full of surreal, almost procedurally generated names and nicknames, and they are part of how the sport tells stories ([Nick Cummings 2026, 52:05](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=3125)).

## Assembled text: templates, grammars and fragments that know themselves

Prose is harder to generate than terrain. Bruno Dias notes that terrain can be simplified into stylised one-metre blocks and players find the result charming, but language has no comparable simplification, and players feel talked down to by simplified prose ([Bruno Dias 2016, 4:11](https://youtu.be/UGPkEWqwSAY?t=251)). Dias names three historical approaches: machine learning, which at the time was resource-hungry and hard to control; plain, matter-of-fact text that exposes a rich world model, as Dwarf Fortress does, where the simulation is the star and the text is a cheap window onto it; and assemblage of authored chunks, which he chose for Voyageur as the pragmatic, shippable option ([Bruno Dias 2016, 5:49](https://youtu.be/UGPkEWqwSAY?t=349)). Darius Kazemi draws a similar line for long-form text, between a linguistic approach that trains on books and a simulationist one that is essentially a roguelike whose renderer outputs prose; he favours the latter ([Darius Kazemi 2017, 30:25](https://youtu.be/CLi4PWxDmAI?t=1825)). This section covers assemblage; the next two cover where the words come from and statistical methods.

The core of assemblage is old. Aaron A. Reed traces it to Christopher Strachey's 1952 love-letter generator for the Manchester computer, which filled template sentences with random words from lists of nouns and adjectives ([Aaron A. Reed 2023, 3:47](https://youtu.be/CE7o3GGif30?t=227)). Modern template systems and context-free grammars such as Tracery work the same way: a grammar of rules that expand into other rules, bottoming out in hand-written word lists picked at random ([Everest Pipkin 2019, 6:33](https://youtu.be/IYNKs8vfocc?t=393)).

### Two load-bearing ideas

The first is about where generated text should sit. Zack Johnson argues that funny procedural text lives between two poles. Pure random generation, such as Markov chains or recurrent neural networks, is funny mostly because it is nonsense, which makes it hard to use for anything; a canned joke is only ever exactly as funny as its source. Kingdom of Loathing aims for the space between ([Zack Johnson 2016, 3:36](https://youtu.be/jNUMRG_tvrY?t=216)).

The second is that fragments become far more useful when the generator knows something about them. Reed points out that procedural text is gibberish to the system deploying it, and that fixing even part of that is a multiplier ([Aaron A. Reed 2020, 17:30](https://youtu.be/x0Xh4oCX9t0?t=1050)). In Subcutanean he ran lexical tools over minor sentence variants to detect negative sentiment, length and simile use, then gave each generated book a chance of a pessimist narrator, or one who favours or avoids similes, rambles, or takes the shortest phrasing; trivial variations became characterization. He says the heuristics came mostly from gut instinct plus whatever text-analysis functions were available ([Aaron A. Reed 2020, 17:30](https://youtu.be/x0Xh4oCX9t0?t=1050)). His other projects push the same idea: in 18 Cadence, fragments know their history, so when combined they replace repeated nouns with pronouns and group sensibly, and in Ice-Bound, story elements are tagged with themes (dedication, family, fragility) so the AI collaborator can notice when the player emphasises, contrasts or ignores one ([Aaron A. Reed 2020, 20:08](https://youtu.be/x0Xh4oCX9t0?t=1208)).

> If your code understanding anything about the text it has that can be a massively useful multiplier. — [Aaron A. Reed 2020, 17:30](https://youtu.be/x0Xh4oCX9t0?t=1050)

Kate Compton shows a cheap way to give text that knowledge. Hip Chef wanted recipes to know that kumquat is citrus and duck is poultry, so ingredient categories could trend and vegan or kosher restaurants could exclude items. Rather than build bigger data structures, she embeds HTML-style tags inline in the grammar text and strips them out after generation, leaving the tags as metadata and the rest as display text ([Kate Compton 2016, 26:15](https://youtu.be/isB82kORimk?t=1575)).

### The machinery in practice

Shipped games use small, specific mechanisms:

- **Metadata-driven combat lines.** Kingdom of Loathing assembles combat messages from per-monster metadata (a gender pronoun and a single attack verb, which takes an *s* for present tense), a hard-coded body-part list and random pain and impact noises, so fights do not repeat the same sentence. It was easy to extend, for example by swapping hit noises for a squeaky hammer; the body part "bung" turned up in nearly every early press screenshot ([Zack Johnson 2016, 6:21](https://youtu.be/jNUMRG_tvrY?t=381)).
- **Markup that points into the world.** Duskers' logs use a small markup language to substitute procedurally generated ship names, and the named ship is then placed in the world for the player to find. Because names change each run, some players went looking for a ship from a previous run, which Tim Keenan says was confusing but also fun ([Tim Keenan 2017, 17:08](https://youtu.be/G5rq5ei2Lec?t=1028)).
- **Grammars with game-state macros.** Alexander Birke's Sea of Rifts generates narrative content as cheaply as possible: long lists for rare crew conversation topics like insults, ship names from an adjective plus Royal Navy names taken from Wikipedia, Tracery with custom macros that inject game state, and place names concatenated from fragments of Danish city names ([Alexander Birke 2024, 17:58](https://youtu.be/0jFzBf0mCRY?t=1078)).
- **The minimal grammar.** Ada Null describes Kiss Garden's stanzas as simple fill-in-the-blank grammars with some variation, no rare paths and no tonal divergence, the "B minus student's" generator. It is enough to reach differentiation without uniqueness, helped by a disaffected narrator whose word choice lets the text blur together ([Ada Null 2025, 6:18](https://youtu.be/VzoruhRyvqQ?t=378)).
- **Counted forms.** Kingdom of Loathing's haiku mode needed a function counting syllables in numbers (the team argued over how to say 108), haiku variants for each syllable length, and a syllable count for every item name, thousands of them, because the mode was available everywhere ([Zack Johnson 2016, 10:56](https://youtu.be/jNUMRG_tvrY?t=656)).

### From concatenation to templates: Caves of Qud

Caves of Qud's message system shows why the machinery has to grow. Brian Bucklew and Corey Frang describe messages that began as plain string concatenation, which worked for "the snapjaw closes the door" and broke at once for "the Mehmet closes the door". The fix was a simple template with a tag marking an object as having a proper name, so the article drops ([Brian Bucklew and Corey Frang 2026, 1:32:35](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=5555)). That turned out to matter far more after 1.0, when players persistently asked for Chinese, Brazilian Portuguese, Turkish and Russian versions of a game with hundreds of thousands of words, many of them procedurally composited ([Brian Bucklew and Corey Frang 2026, 1:30:30](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=5430)).

The current syntax is concrete enough to copy. Placeholders are wrapped in equals signs; a period separates the argument alias from the replacer name; a colon passes a literal from the template text, such as the verb "take" to the "does" replacer, giving "the watervine farmer takes" or "you take", so a translation can swap the verb while the replacer still handles articles, plurality and conjugation; and a hash refers to an argument passed in from code, such as a direction ([Brian Bucklew and Corey Frang 2026, 1:43:16](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=6196)). The piece the team calls essential for localization is chaining: a pipe passes one replacer's output into the next, so an object's name can be pluralised and then title-cased. One Englishism survives: replacers capitalise their output when the placeholder's first letter is capitalised, because so many templates were piping to "capitalize" at the start of sentences ([Brian Bucklew and Corey Frang 2026, 1:44:57](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=6297)). Chaining is also what made Turkish possible. Turkish is agglutinative, so "with his hands" is one word, built by passing "hands" through a possessive processor and then an instrumental one; Turkish also puts the verb last and drops pronouns, so the localizers added a "maybe subject" replacer that has no use in English ([Brian Bucklew and Corey Frang 2026, 1:53:54](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=6834)).

Not every problem is solved. Compton calls grammatical gender in Tracery "a real pain": her attempt at French nouns and gendered adjectives for a restaurant generator turned into the grammar equivalent of a giant if statement, and she invites someone to build a tool that tracks gender automatically ([Kate Compton 2016, 31:09](https://youtu.be/isB82kORimk?t=1869)). If you expect to localize, plan for processors like Qud's from the start rather than concatenating strings.

### Flavour text as an end in itself

Some generated text has no job beyond being enjoyed, and that can be enough. Leonard Richardson points to NetHack's hallucination names, which show a random unrelated thing each time you look at a monster (a rat might be a Ravenous Bugblatter Beast or Godzilla); designers may call such lists bloat, but he argues there is a rarely made kind of game where glimpses into varied worlds are the point ([Leonard Richardson 2017, 9:06](https://youtu.be/ntVjLNl2_ro?t=546)). His own robotfindskitten descriptions were often made by taking a mundane thing in view, like a bottle of hair conditioner, and changing words until it looked weird ([Leonard Richardson 2017, 16:46](https://youtu.be/ntVjLNl2_ro?t=1006)). Ray reads Caves of Qud's "whip up a meal", which throws random and often absurd ingredients into the pot description, as a storyteller's hyperbole that adds to the game's tall-tale tone ([Ray 2025, 6:18](https://youtu.be/rPhXTcVVJmo?t=378)). Matt Carney highlights Amber Spire, a city builder by Nick Tringali and Dr. Holly Nelson, whose building descriptions come in mixed voices, from first-person quotes to overheard remarks to near-academic text, and which together convey a cultural history ([Matt Carney 2026, 22:09](https://youtu.be/SU-VcmsOvZo?t=1329)).

## Choosing the source: corpora, found text and curation

Whatever the technique, generated text comes from other text. Everest Pipkin walks through templates, cut-ups, Markov chains and neural networks and makes the same point about each: none produces text from nothing, so the provenance of the input determines what the generator can say ([Everest Pipkin 2019, 9:11](https://youtu.be/IYNKs8vfocc?t=551)). That makes choosing the source, the *corpus*, the decision that matters most. Pipkin ties "curation" to the Latin for care and argues the care belongs to the material the work is made from, not only to the output; in a hand-written grammar it happens naturally as you pick favourite words, and even with Markov chains you choose the input for the feeling it produces ([Everest Pipkin 2019, 10:39](https://youtu.be/IYNKs8vfocc?t=639)).

> Picking the right source material, the material that feels right, is perhaps like the most important decision in generative text. — [Everest Pipkin 2019, 10:39](https://youtu.be/IYNKs8vfocc?t=639)

### Why big generic corpora go bland

Pipkin's warning is that a model sounds like the average of its source: trained on Reddit it sounds like Reddit, a Twitter bot sounds like Twitter, random Project Gutenberg pulls give a mushy, well-to-do 18th-century feel, and averaging any of these yields blandness ([Everest Pipkin 2019, 15:40](https://youtu.be/IYNKs8vfocc?t=940)). The bigger and more complex the system, the more invisible the author's choice of material becomes and the further the output drifts from the intended feeling; GPT-2, trained on millions of articles linked from Reddit posts with more than three upvotes, is the extreme case ([Everest Pipkin 2019, 11:50](https://youtu.be/IYNKs8vfocc?t=710)). Kate Compton arrives at the same point from small word lists. A shared colour list turned out less useful than she expected, because a Jane Austen generator wants "ecru" and "daffodil" and a Lovecraft one wants "squamous"; dropping in red, green and blue cuts out the fun ([Kate Compton 2016, 30:57](https://youtu.be/isB82kORimk?t=1857)).

The alternative Pipkin recommends is to build your own corpus from niche sources you love, such as old forums, DIY resources or gardening comment sections, spaces that never make it into precompiled datasets because nobody cares about them as much as you do ([Everest Pipkin 2019, 20:02](https://youtu.be/IYNKs8vfocc?t=1202)). A curated corpus gives hyper-specific control over tone, content, ethics and language while the generator still surprises you with specifics ([Everest Pipkin 2019, 20:52](https://youtu.be/IYNKs8vfocc?t=1252)). It also lets you treat source authors as collaborators: Pipkin's book *I've never picked a protected flower* has an 18-page thank-you section listing the usernames of the forum posters whose titles it uses, something no large dataset does ([Everest Pipkin 2019, 22:03](https://youtu.be/IYNKs8vfocc?t=1323)).

### Curation as craft

The practitioners who use found text treat building the corpus as design work:

- **Half your own, half matched.** Jason Grinblat built Caves of Qud's book corpus from about 45,000 words of the game's own text (static books, NPC dialogue, quest text, descriptions, even help files, which produces in-game books that talk about Caves of Qud) and a similar amount of public-domain 19th-century books chosen to match the tone, such as a physics text and *Zoological Mythology* ([Jason Grinblat 2016, 10:31](https://youtu.be/zDTQM0Ipiz4?t=631)).
- **Split by voice.** Botnik split X-Files transcripts into separate corpora for Mulder's lines, Scully's lines and stage directions, each its own generative source, and did the same for Dear Abby with one corpus for questions and one for answers ([Botnik 2017, 8:10](https://youtu.be/IujSOW1OMWk?t=490)).
- **Mash the unrelated.** Combining two unrelated corpora in one predictive keyboard, such as Amazon reviews of P90X and Morrissey lyrics, produces comic mashups ([Botnik 2017, 43:57](https://youtu.be/IujSOW1OMWk?t=2637)).
- **Score found lines against a form.** Jamie Brew's Robot Karaoke models a song's lyrics as words with syllable counts, stress patterns and vowel sounds, picks found lines with the same syllable count as each original line, scores them by phonetic similarity, and hands the result to a performer to sing on the spot ([Jamie Brew 2025, 6:03](https://youtu.be/685wpSUVw9s?t=363)). The found text comes from Craigslist ads, Yelp reviews, tax forms, fraudulent emails, archived early-internet banner ads and audience submissions such as crowdsourced fears ([Jamie Brew 2025, 28:12](https://youtu.be/685wpSUVw9s?t=1692)).
- **Parse actions out of prose.** Max Hawkins mines possible actions from books and web text with constituency parsing: extract the verb phrases, lemmatise them and replace pronouns with "you", so "she went to the park and thought she was a tree" becomes "go to the park and think you are a tree" ([Max Hawkins 2019, 22:57](https://youtu.be/anwk8b7c_s0?t=1377)).

### Other mined sources

Text can be mined for structure as well as words. Tyler Coleman generates items from adjective-noun pairs in public-domain books: word vectors match the noun to an item type and the adjectives become value modifiers, so "poor little feet" becomes boots with better detection, and when no item fits the noun a spelling-similarity fallback picks the closest-looking word, giving a "wise little antidote" ([Tyler Coleman 2026, 5:33:35](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=20015)). Ezra Szanton's most exciting open idea is a roguelike deckbuilder that uses a real-world network (Wikipedia links, map distances, IMDb's actors and films) as its card content and synergy structure, so content already exists and players bring mental models; the hard part is a rule set that turns the network's qualities into play ([Ezra Szanton 2025, 26:23](https://youtu.be/JfNeYtH7xI4?t=1583)). Neutrinowatch's "Daily Blast" scrapes about 50 RSS feeds for headlines containing words like blast, slam and eviscerate, plus a good-news and a human-interest headline, and has two AI voices read them ([Jeff Emtman and Martin Austwick 2024, 23:08](https://youtu.be/1sZlIfCcz_c?t=1388)). Leigh Alexander's McMansion pulls room images from a search API using per-room search strings and dithers them client-side into a unified vintage Macintosh look, while cautioning that the cost would be high at scale and the images are taken without regard to provenance, which would need to change ([Leigh Alexander 2023, 22:16](https://youtu.be/NjYS8XmeaiY?t=1336)).

### Constrained forms

Constraints are another way to shape a source. Julian Day names cut-up poetry, cutting source poems into pieces and reassembling them by hand or by algorithm, as a constraint that suits procedural generation ([Julian Day 2020, 29:16](https://youtu.be/aBbaUSWFQPM?t=1756)). At the far end he describes Christian Bök's Xenotext, which needed a substitution cipher under which both a source poem and its encoded output are meaningful; Bök wrote a program to search for word pairs that decode to other real words, then chose a cipher and wrote the poem ([Julian Day 2020, 21:39](https://youtu.be/aBbaUSWFQPM?t=1299)).

The common lesson is that the corpus is a design artifact. Decide what voice you want, build the source that has it, and keep a record of where it came from.

## Statistical text: Markov chains and language models

Statistical methods learn word patterns from a corpus instead of following authored rules. A *Markov chain* records which words follow each short run of words (the prefix) in the source and generates by walking those transitions at random. Language models such as GPT-2 do something similar at vastly larger scale. A Markov chain's weakness is meaning: its output can be grammatical yet semantically odd ([Jason Grinblat 2016, 4:12](https://youtu.be/zDTQM0Ipiz4?t=252)). The talks suggest using statistical text where that weakness becomes a feature.

### Caves of Qud's library

Jason Grinblat is the clearest case. He wanted Caves of Qud's library to feel like texts from across the ages, half-decipherable through linguistic drift and transliteration, full of fractured meaning and half-remembered myth, and realised that grammatical but semantically odd Markov text produces exactly that ([Jason Grinblat 2016, 4:12](https://youtu.be/zDTQM0Ipiz4?t=252)). The implementation is simple enough to reproduce:

- **Sentences.** While building the chain, keep a separate list of prefixes that begin sentences. Start from a random one and walk until you hit a period, with a fallback that stops after 50 words, which rarely triggers ([Jason Grinblat 2016, 11:51](https://youtu.be/zDTQM0Ipiz4?t=711)).
- **Paragraphs and books.** A paragraph is three to six sentences; a book is eight to thirty paragraphs, laid out with the game's existing formatting tools ([Jason Grinblat 2016, 11:51](https://youtu.be/zDTQM0Ipiz4?t=711)).
- **Titles.** Walk the chain two to five times and shave undesirable words (pronouns, conjunctions and the like, from a static list of about 30) off the start and end, so "at the foot of a sickly tree until" becomes a usable title. Grinblat's first attempt filled templates like "The X of Y", but a bug let non-template titles through and they were better ([Jason Grinblat 2016, 15:03](https://youtu.be/zDTQM0Ipiz4?t=903)).
- **Secrets.** To hide real lore in the noise, write each secret as a whole phrase after a common prefix hook, add it to the corpus, and add a rule that stops the chain from splitting it into two-word units. The proof of concept points to an artifact pistol, the Ruin of House Isner, on one of about 18,000 map screens, with secrets that give distances from static landmarks, "east of Joppa some six parasangs", where a parasang is about one world-map tile ([Jason Grinblat 2016, 20:24](https://youtu.be/zDTQM0Ipiz4?t=1224)).

Grinblat's open problem is that each kind of lore needs its own hand-crafted secret generator, because secrets must be well-formed English for the chain to ingest them meaningfully; he wants a general way to turn Qud's procedural elements into secrets, plus thematic sub-corpora and paragraphs ([Jason Grinblat 2016, 22:58](https://youtu.be/zDTQM0Ipiz4?t=1378)).

### How players read it

The Markov books need not read as a failure to write enough. Ray notes that Qud shows handwritten books with yellow titles and Markov books with white titles, and reads the white ones as signalling that those books are irrelevant to the player character's tale, part of a mythic rather than literal experience ([Ray 2025, 5:14](https://youtu.be/rPhXTcVVJmo?t=314)). Younès Rabii describes the mix as crystals in a cloud of smoke: most books are readable nonsense, but occasional handwritten ones hold real clues to interesting objects, which rewards exploration ([Younès Rabii 2025, 27:14](https://youtu.be/BJ_84d7v3K4?t=1634)). Together they suggest a pattern: statistical text works as a medium of noise in which a small amount of authored signal can be found. For comedy, Joe Sondow observes that Markov bots spun off from his hand-written Star Trek parody accounts produce a different quality of comedy from the originals, not a copy of it ([Thomas Robertson et al. 2017, 24:16](https://youtu.be/H6fPIhLoA1Y?t=1456)), which fits Zack Johnson's point, made under assembled text above, that random text is funny mainly as nonsense ([Zack Johnson 2016, 3:36](https://youtu.be/jNUMRG_tvrY?t=216)).

### Language models against templates

The disagreement over language models is about what each method is good at over time. Robin Sloan argues that language-model output outlasts even nested templates, because a template's seams show: read one output and it is interesting, read five and you sense the pattern and the pattern becomes the thing you enjoy, not the words. GPT-2, in his view, is also a template, but one as large as the language ([Robin Sloan 2019, 18:33](https://youtu.be/cIpErjWBqm0?t=1113)). His practical suggestion is to use a language model as a description engine, since describing things is what such models do best: run a prompt like "the village of Firepuddle was known for" many times, filter and store the results offline or generate them live, and even stringently filtered output keeps a diversity a hand-written template lacks ([Robin Sloan 2019, 23:24](https://youtu.be/cIpErjWBqm0?t=1404)).

> I think you always see the seams. I think you read one and it's interesting, I think you read five and you start to sense the pattern. — [Robin Sloan 2019, 18:33](https://youtu.be/cIpErjWBqm0?t=1113)

Brianna McHorse and Chris Foster grant the strengths: generative AI is expressive, responds to language input and offers far more possibilities than a procedural system for similar effort, which also leaves an unbounded space that is hard to guide toward good stories ([Brianna McHorse and Chris Foster 2023, 14:45](https://youtu.be/aJC3ioashbs?t=885)). Their central objection is consistency. Language models are good at capturing moments and bad at coherence over time, and games need constraints applied consistently, with stories that unfold through time; Foster argues unbounded agency is make-believe, not gameplay ([Brianna McHorse and Chris Foster 2023, 15:30](https://youtu.be/aJC3ioashbs?t=930)). They also list the ethical risks: models magnify bias and default to stereotypes, are trained on unlicensed work that can leak into output, and present hallucinations as knowledge. Hidden Door chose the public-domain Wizard of Oz as its first world on purpose, and McHorse urges thinking through ethics at the start rather than bolting it on ([Brianna McHorse and Chris Foster 2023, 11:24](https://youtu.be/aJC3ioashbs?t=684)).

### Where each fits

Read together, these positions point to a division of labour rather than a winner.
