Markov chains suit text whose meaning is meant to be lost or half-legible, and can carry hidden authored signal if you protect it from being split ([Jason Grinblat 2016, 4:12](https://youtu.be/zDTQM0Ipiz4?t=252); [Jason Grinblat 2016, 20:24](https://youtu.be/zDTQM0Ipiz4?t=1224); [Younès Rabii 2025, 27:14](https://youtu.be/BJ_84d7v3K4?t=1634)). Language models suit short descriptions that can be generated and filtered ahead of time, where seams would show in a template and where inconsistency over time does not matter ([Robin Sloan 2019, 23:24](https://youtu.be/cIpErjWBqm0?t=1404); [Robin Sloan 2019, 18:33](https://youtu.be/cIpErjWBqm0?t=1113)). Neither suits text that must stay consistent with game state across a run; that remains the job of templates and simulation, covered in the section on assembled text above ([Brianna McHorse and Chris Foster 2023, 15:30](https://youtu.be/aJC3ioashbs?t=930)). Pipkin's warning about generic corpora applies most strongly to large models ([Everest Pipkin 2019, 15:40](https://youtu.be/IYNKs8vfocc?t=940)).

## Generated history and culture: pasts that leave traces

Generating a world's past is expensive, and a history the player never meets is wasted. The talks that make it work treat history as a source of things in the present: buildings, items, enemies, factions and rumours the player can find and act on.

### History as the driver of the present

Caves of Qud's villages show the principle. Each village is driven by its own generated history, which shapes its architecture style, culture, quests, NPCs and even proverbs; the developers describe it as an amalgam of all their procedural systems, with one example village of snapjaws, normally early-game enemies, who have settled down ([Jason Grinblat et al. 2018, 13:19](https://youtu.be/owmGknfj6H4?t=799)). Each village also has a generated signature dish, such as meat apple baklava, that grants a generated status effect when eaten, tying cooking to village generation ([Jason Grinblat et al. 2018, 23:00](https://youtu.be/owmGknfj6H4?t=1380)).

Florence Smith Nicholls offers a frame from archaeology: *object biographies*, the full lifecycle and network of interactions an object went through, not just the object as found. For a chair that means its material, where the wood came from, who made it with what tools, whether it was reused, who owned or traded it, and whether it ended in the ground or a museum ([Florence Smith Nicholls 2022, 1:54](https://youtu.be/IanNZxUaVQs?t=114)). She notes Qud already does a version of this, placing sultans' relics in their reliquaries with decorations that can relate to their history ([Florence Smith Nicholls 2022, 3:01](https://youtu.be/IanNZxUaVQs?t=181)). Her own extension is to make objects physically shaped by history and fragmented, so the order in which the player examines the parts changes the biography they construct: a book in a village destroyed by animals, its pages ripped out for a nest, tells a different story depending on which pages you read first ([Florence Smith Nicholls 2022, 8:31](https://youtu.be/IanNZxUaVQs?t=511)).

### Worked example: Qud's sultans

Jason Grinblat's procedural history system in Caves of Qud is the most complete case in the talks, and its design decisions are worth taking in order.

**Constrain the scope.** A full history is colossal, so Qud centres each world's history on five ancient sultans from an era before most of the handwritten lore; each world seed produces a different five ([Jason Grinblat 2017, 3:13](https://youtu.be/ClGAApZYIvI?t=193)).

**Build it event by event.** History is generated one event at a time (birth, siege, marriage, death), each like a chapter in a ruler's biography. When the marriage event was first added, a bug made it the only event, and sultans married cats, baboons and a robot ([Jason Grinblat 2017, 9:28](https://youtu.be/ClGAApZYIvI?t=568)). The sultans share one timeline, so earlier sultans' actions, such as renaming a place after an epic battle, carry into later ones' histories ([Jason Grinblat 2017, 31:30](https://youtu.be/ClGAApZYIvI?t=1890)).

**Give each figure a theme.** Every sultan has a domain (jewels, ice, starlight, scholarship, might) that flavours their events and works like an epithet in epic poetry, making them memorable and blurring history into myth. A sultan born with emeralds on his eyes later traps a victim in a jewel and founds a hermitage for chanting to rubies; another's weddings all happen in blocks of ice ([Jason Grinblat 2017, 9:10](https://youtu.be/ClGAApZYIvI?t=550)).

**Do not impose an arc.** Qud deliberately applies no narrative structure such as the hero's journey, and can afford to because the system is off the critical path: a bizarre life is fine, since there will be another next game. One of the few constraints is that each must become sultan at some point, which once produced a 100-year-old who assassinated his father, took the throne and died the next day ([Jason Grinblat 2017, 20:01](https://youtu.be/ClGAApZYIvI?t=1201)).

**Turn the history into things.** This is where the cost pays off:

- **Legendary items.** Items named in history are instantiated in the world. A sultan saved by dogs lost the axe "Freezing Ages, Boon of Dogs" at the Hippodrome; the player gets quests to recover it, and it deals +5 cold damage and gives +200 reputation with dogs, with a description carved with icicles and dogs ([Jason Grinblat 2017, 12:13](https://youtu.be/ClGAApZYIvI?t=733)).
- **Cults.** Generated cults form around sultans, named after the sultan or an epithet, and history sites are populated with cultists; at the Hippodrome, aggressive dog cultists guard the axe, and the player can fight them or find another way in ([Jason Grinblat 2017, 16:24](https://youtu.be/ClGAApZYIvI?t=984)).
- **Legendary monsters with grudges.** Elsewhere in Qud, unique monsters, marked in magenta, carry faction relationships from past deeds: a chrome idol hated by two groups for torching their villages, a goat folk shaman hated by bears for slaying a leader ([Jason Grinblat and Nick DeCapua 2017, 52:25](https://youtu.be/kDKQM27U-Nc?t=3145)).
- **Secrets to trade.** Discovered locations are written into the journal as secrets that can be sold to NPCs interested in that kind of knowledge ([Jason Grinblat and Nick DeCapua 2017, 32:03](https://youtu.be/kDKQM27U-Nc?t=1923)).
- **Conflicting records.** Ray points out that the sultan shrines depict an item, location and event you can actually find, but murals in the Tomb of the Eaters, closer in time to the events, show them very differently, which makes the player wonder how real the shrine history is ([Ray 2025, 10:22](https://youtu.be/rPhXTcVVJmo?t=622)).

History can also leak into the present in ways no one planned. Main characters in Qud are generated with backstories that make them admired or disliked by random factions among about 70; in 1-2% of games this makes the farmer Mehmet disliked by the Fellowship of Wardens, Warden Ualraig kills him, and sometimes all of Joppa erupts. Grinblat calls it awkward in the fiction and a big gameplay leak, since it locks players out of the starting side quest ([Jason Grinblat 2021, 19:47](https://youtu.be/kvCky6BbTuE?t=1187)), yet he also finds it interesting and calls it even money whether the team fixes it. The more connections a generated past has to the present, the more of these you should expect. Not every such leak is a defect to be engineered out; the chapter's last section returns to unintended output that players find meaning in.

### Myths, religions and rituals

Other projects generate culture rather than chronicle. Tarn Adams described Dwarf Fortress's planned myth and magic generator, which would create whole mythologies with concrete in-world requirements: a rune stone that must be carved from a rare stone under the stars is something you would actually have to do ([Zach Adams and Tarn Adams 2016, 26:41](https://youtu.be/Zh6dnx9FM1g?t=1601)). Smith Nicholls mentions Mark R Johnson's writing on "qualitative procedural generation", generating abstract content such as religion and asking how it shapes the culture around it ([Florence Smith Nicholls 2022, 12:16](https://youtu.be/IanNZxUaVQs?t=736)).

Spencer Egart's ritual generator is the most implementable of these. It takes tagged lists of verbs and nouns (which may already exist in a game that uses an action pattern), associates them with effect parameters such as element, target and magnitude, and picks steps that satisfy the effect's requirements; the larger the combination space, the more varied the rituals ([Spencer Egart 2019, 5:56](https://youtu.be/q4Tf0vf2kiI?t=356)). Functional steps (draw the fire rune to set the element, speak the target's name to set the target) are then padded with flavour steps such as stepping in compass directions and drawing circles, so the whole reads as ritual ([Spencer Egart 2019, 9:51](https://youtu.be/q4Tf0vf2kiI?t=591)). A generated entry like "a charm to bring fortune to your ally" chains shattering a pearl, shouting the ally's name, facing west, burning thyme and drawing a rune ([Spencer Egart 2019, 2:25](https://youtu.be/q4Tf0vf2kiI?t=145)). The pattern, meaningful steps hidden among decorative ones, is reusable wherever you want generated procedures to feel cultural.

History can also be lived rather than written. In Bad News, every business in the town was started by a simulated person who had the idea, and businesses persist, close or change hands over the simulation; their names come from real corpora of bar and hospital names ([Bad News team 2016, 17:35](https://youtu.be/XFFyN10o87I?t=1055)).

### Comparing generators

Mike Cook suggests a way to study all of this: compare two games' generators the way you would compare two cities. Dwarf Fortress and Caves of Qud are like London and Paris; they share a lot because both generate history, so the interesting question is what differs in the character of how each handles it ([Mike Cook 2026, 16:22](https://youtu.be/nOGNdrjm8ek?t=982)). Applied to your own game, ask what your history generator is *for*: which traces it leaves, and what the player can do with them.

## Generated systems: economies, tech trees and societies

A generated history is one structure that can differ from world to world. Economies, technologies and societies are others. Most generated content is a thing the player looks at: a name, a room, a monster. A generated *system* is different. When the structure of an economy or a research tree changes from one world to the next, each world can imply a different kind of universe ([Dustin Freeman 2020, 11:19](https://youtu.be/8HDmpu7Kp-A?t=679)). Two talks give full worked examples, one for economies and one for technology, and both build their systems as graphs.

### Economies as goods graphs

Mark Gritter's Emoji Economy generates toy economies in four steps: build a graph of goods flows, maximise a utility function with diminishing returns over the choices the graph allows, make altered regional copies, and find trade routes that restore the utility the regions lost ([Mark Gritter 2020, 1:18](https://youtu.be/Q_MFTUYnaf0?t=78)). The steps in turn:

- **The goods graph.** Nodes are goods or processes. The graph starts from natural goods (his example uses plants such as melons and lemons) and ends in a consumption sink (pie). His prototype has only two transformation types: factories, which combine two units into one new unit, and processing plants, which split one unit into its parts ([Mark Gritter 2020, 2:20](https://youtu.be/Q_MFTUYnaf0?t=140)).
- **Utility.** Diminishing marginal utility means a region gains less from each extra unit of the same good; the generator chooses how the graph's goods are used so as to maximise that utility ([Mark Gritter 2020, 1:18](https://youtu.be/Q_MFTUYnaf0?t=78)).
- **Regions.** Gritter makes regional differences by deleting parts of each region's copy of the graph. One region cannot grow apples; another lacks the infrastructure for juice. Each deletion lowers that region's utility and so gives it a reason to trade. In the simplest case, if A can make juice but not butter and B the reverse, trading equal amounts leaves both better off ([Mark Gritter 2020, 7:00](https://youtu.be/Q_MFTUYnaf0?t=420)).
- **Trade.** A search for trade routes that restore utility then produces the network.

Breaking nine regions and running the trade step gave a dense, sensible trade network with real variety. Gritter is clear about the limits: every trade is bidirectional, so the triangle trades of real economies never appear, and there are no transport costs or geography, which he names as the obvious next additions ([Mark Gritter 2020, 9:28](https://youtu.be/Q_MFTUYnaf0?t=568)).

A generated economy also gives you a source of play beyond buying and selling. Robin Mendoza proposes using price movements as passive quest hooks. Instead of an NPC handing out a task, the player notices a price moving, guesses what is happening in the world, and chooses to step in before the facts are known. Acting on a hunch carries its own risk and reward, tips could be bought and sold, and prices could reveal secrets or what NPCs and factions are doing ([Robin Mendoza 2024, 3:52](https://youtu.be/ZtXGg6ECwQ8?t=232)). This only works if the prices come from an economy the player can learn to read, which is the case for building one like Gritter's.

### Tech trees as nodes, weights and topology

Dustin Freeman gives a vocabulary for generated technology trees: *nodes* (the technologies), *connections* whose weights encode how hard a technology is to research given what you already know, and *topology*, the overall shape. A generator can vary each of these separately. Two trees can share nodes but connect them differently (different topology), or share a topology but differ in research difficulty (different weights) ([Dustin Freeman 2020, 1:28](https://youtu.be/8HDmpu7Kp-A?t=88)). He contrasts game trees with real research, where the topology, the weights and even the set of possible technologies are unknown in advance, and where technologies fail or go unadopted for reasons no one could predict. His examples are the Microsoft Surface touch table, which worked but was not taken up, and airships, which exist but which nobody seems to want ([Dustin Freeman 2020, 2:01](https://youtu.be/8HDmpu7Kp-A?t=121)).

Freeman surveys how existing games vary a tree, and each varies a different part of it:

- **Sword of the Stars** keeps a fixed topology but rolls, for each player at the start of the game, whether each connection exists, so every player gets a different tree ([Dustin Freeman 2020, 4:23](https://youtu.be/8HDmpu7Kp-A?t=263)).
- **Limit Theory** planned a system where researching a node eventually spawns child nodes that are variations of it, so the player grows the topology as they play, from a fixed core set. Freeman likens it to dog breeding, but the game was cancelled, so how it would have felt is unknown ([Dustin Freeman 2020, 4:48](https://youtu.be/8HDmpu7Kp-A?t=288)).
- **Alpha Centauri's** blind research mode hides a fixed tree and lets the player choose only a focus (discover, explore, conquer or build), after which a random technology from that area unlocks. The hidden topology itself never changes ([Dustin Freeman 2020, 5:07](https://youtu.be/8HDmpu7Kp-A?t=307)).
- **Stellaris** offers three random options drawn from tiered technologies, with access to a tier gated on researching some number of technologies from the tier before. This limits choice at any one moment, but for Freeman it does not feel like research, and choosing is not exciting ([Dustin Freeman 2020, 5:24](https://youtu.be/8HDmpu7Kp-A?t=324)).

### Feasibility as the thing that makes worlds differ

Freeman's own generator adds a further dimension. It gives each technology a *feasibility category*: trivial or accidental (the wheel), a project (nuclear power), civilization-scale (fixing climate change), barely functional (curing cancer), a crapshoot (telepathy), a costly crapshoot (nuclear fusion), or possible but undesired ([Dustin Freeman 2020, 9:22](https://youtu.be/8HDmpu7Kp-A?t=562)). He finds the last the most interesting: a technology that could exist but that no one wants, waiting for a cultural shift or other surprise to make it real. His historical case is the Ottoman Empire not adopting the printing press for centuries, for reasons that are unclear ([Dustin Freeman 2020, 9:36](https://youtu.be/8HDmpu7Kp-A?t=576)).

The labels are what make one generated universe feel unlike another. In one of his outputs AI is undesired, bioengineering a costly crapshoot and cybernetics trivial; in another AI is trivial and cybernetics a crapshoot. Freeman argues these evocative, differing universes are more interesting than a tree with merely random topology ([Dustin Freeman 2020, 11:19](https://youtu.be/8HDmpu7Kp-A?t=679)). This is the oatmeal problem from earlier in the chapter, solved at the level of a whole system: random topology changes the tree without changing what kind of world it implies, while feasibility labels change the world's character.

### Flavour against balance

Freeman names the cost of this kind of variety. Stellaris originally gave civilizations different faster-than-light methods but removed them for balance, because defending against warp, wormholes and hyperlanes at once was hard. He calls that an unfortunate trade, because what excites him about technology is the evocativeness of the universe a tech system implies, not the balance choices ([Dustin Freeman 2020, 6:21](https://youtu.be/8HDmpu7Kp-A?t=381)). If your generated systems make worlds asymmetric, expect the same pressure to even them out, and decide in advance which you value more. Freeman's position is one designer's preference; a competitive multiplayer game may reasonably decide the other way.

### Social structure from one repeated action

Generated societies can come from the same idea of one rule applied at several scales. Jonathan Lessard, drawing on the book *Stone Age Economics*, models social structure with a single gift-exchange action applied fractally: exchange within families builds clans, exchange between clans builds tribes, and exchange between tribes builds something like a kingdom. He likes it for systems modelling because one action piles up into a full social structure. He admits it does not show much in play, but it makes the world feel alive with relationships ([Jonathan Lessard 2023, 14:10](https://youtu.be/D8A9dpITLAU?t=850)).

### Where generated systems could go

Freeman closes with two open directions for tech trees: *cross-domain discovery*, where research in one domain yields technology in another (the microwave came out of communications research), and *domain progression*, where a technology's substrate changes over time, as computing moved from wood to metal gears, vacuum tubes, transistors and perhaps qubits ([Dustin Freeman 2020, 11:38](https://youtu.be/8HDmpu7Kp-A?t=698)). Both would make the generated graph less tidy, which, by his account of real research, is closer to the truth.

## Quests: defining, generating and allocating them

A quest generator has two jobs that are easy to confuse. One is deciding what a quest is made of, so the generator has parts to combine. The other is deciding which quest, and which location, to hand the player right now, without running out or repeating. The talks cover both, and the second turns out to be harder than it looks ([Jurie Horneman 2023, 14:06](https://youtu.be/FV_0rmqxbxw?t=846); [Jurie Horneman 2023, 14:57](https://youtu.be/FV_0rmqxbxw?t=897)).

### A definition you can generate from

Kristen Yu starts from a practical problem: developers and academics define quests differently, which makes procedural quest generation and precise discussion hard. She asked coworkers, including a lead world designer with 15 years of experience, and got different answers or none; the 16 papers on quest generation she read had 16 different definitions ([Kristen Yu 2021, 3:50](https://youtu.be/WutTZ4FCHA8?t=230)). Her synthesis is deliberately general: a quest is a set of tasks the player must complete to earn one or more rewards. Rewards include items and currencies, narrative payoffs such as NPC dialogue or cutscenes, and progression such as XP, skill points or newly unlocked map areas ([Kristen Yu 2021, 4:23](https://youtu.be/WutTZ4FCHA8?t=263)).

Each task is then specified by five fields ([Kristen Yu 2021, 5:18](https://youtu.be/WutTZ4FCHA8?t=318)):

- **Who** can complete it.
- **Objective**: what must be done.
- **Monitoring**: the system that detects whether the task was completed.
- **Presentation**: how the task is shown to the player.
- **Reward**: the task's own reward, which lets you pay out in small amounts as the quest progresses.

Yu stresses that monitoring and presentation are often ignored by academics yet matter a great deal in production ([Kristen Yu 2021, 5:18](https://youtu.be/WutTZ4FCHA8?t=318)). Her worked example is Animal Crossing: New Horizons' 'Angling for Perfection': five tasks (catch 10, 100, 500, 1,000 and 3,000 fish), one player, a system checking catches, a stamp card showing completed tasks with a bubble for current progress, and different rewards per task in Nook Miles and passport titles ([Kristen Yu 2021, 6:21](https://youtu.be/WutTZ4FCHA8?t=381)). If your generator emits all five fields for every task, it emits something the rest of the game can track and display.

### Context and purpose instead of main and side

A definition gives you every possible quest; you still need to narrow it. Yu's Definition-Context-Purpose paradigm treats design as a funnel: the definition covers all possible quests, *context* adds creative and production constraints, and *purpose* states why the quest is in the game. She derived it from thematic analysis of over 13 hours of interviews with 15 developers, and a game can have several overlapping contexts and purposes ([Kristen Yu 2021, 12:03](https://youtu.be/WutTZ4FCHA8?t=723)). This replaces the main/side split, which generated narrative quests fit badly. In her example game, quick fetch quests have one task and exist to encourage exploration, while both the handcrafted main quests and the generated narrative quests exist to tell the story; you can define as many buckets as you need ([Kristen Yu 2021, 17:18](https://youtu.be/WutTZ4FCHA8?t=1038)).

For a generator, her advice is to write the context and purpose down. Her hypothetical generator links quests to tell a secondary story; its stated context covers task types, rewards, presentation, and whether generated quests should look different from handcrafted ones. Writing this down gives other developers on the team the right expectations and counters their own assumptions about what a quest is ([Kristen Yu 2021, 15:48](https://youtu.be/WutTZ4FCHA8?t=948)). She also accepts where her definition leads: by it, Mario 1-1 is a quest, and so is a season pass, even if calling them that is not useful, and you need not use every part of the definition (monitoring, say) when it does not help ([Kristen Yu 2021, 22:39](https://youtu.be/WutTZ4FCHA8?t=1359)).

### Generation pipelines: from a database to the map

One working generator has a simple shape: hand-written quests in a database, broken into parts, scattered over generated space. Francesco Cottone's Chronicles of Stampadia, a paper game with a daily adventure, follows Fallout: The Board Game: quests from a database are split into sub-events and scattered through the dungeon, from the starting room to the farthest room ([Francesco Cottone 2021, 7:25](https://youtu.be/IPMXeSAvtDs?t=445)). Each daily adventure takes no designer time. The algorithm picks quests and sub-quests, fills in their random elements, and places their hotspots on a generated dungeon, and writing a new quest takes a few minutes because it is mostly text ([Francesco Cottone 2021, 13:46](https://youtu.be/IPMXeSAvtDs?t=826)). Scattering has a consequence: players roam out of order, so they meet sub-events out of sequence, and the game needed a memory system to track it. In a paper game that raised the question of how players can store state without knowing what it means ([Francesco Cottone 2021, 7:25](https://youtu.be/IPMXeSAvtDs?t=445)).

Caves of Qud uses quests to point the player outward. Its starting villages usually offer two generated quests, alongside a static quest found in every village, such as finding a forgotten place or recovering a farmer's token tied to a sultan. The quests reveal generated locations, which are written into the journal and can be marked on the map, giving the player reasons to head out into the world ([Jason Grinblat et al. 2018, 26:17](https://youtu.be/owmGknfj6H4?t=1577)). Quest design can also create the world it needs. Qud added shrines, places to pray or desecrate, partly because the procedural quest design needed reasons for players to desecrate statues, for instance out of a vendetta against the faction that worships them ([Jason Grinblat et al. 2018, 50:10](https://youtu.be/owmGknfj6H4?t=3010)). If your quest grammar has a verb, the world needs objects that verb can act on.

### Allocation: who gets the location

Jurie Horneman's talk is about the problem behind all of this: selecting content at runtime is harder than it looks. His case is a big-world RPG where a non-combat class like a bard can talk past fights. There are far more fights than authored quests, so quests come from a pool, chosen to fit the opponent (an ogre or a goblin), and their locations are picked near the player so they are not sent back to the same place. That is two layers of dynamic selection, one for the quest and one for its locations ([Jurie Horneman 2023, 8:08](https://youtu.be/FV_0rmqxbxw?t=488)).

He gives three pieces of engineering for this:

1. **Separate picky from non-picky requests.** A core story quest is *picky*: it needs one specific location, once (the big fight in the fortress). Generic reusable quests are *non-picky*. Keep special locations in a story-only pool until their story quest is done, then release them into the general pool. The story quest always gets its location, and the general pool grows fresher over time ([Jurie Horneman 2023, 12:03](https://youtu.be/FV_0rmqxbxw?t=723)).
2. **Prove the allocator safe by counting.** For every point in the game, there must be at least as many matching locations as quests that could ask for them at the same time. If one quest needs a green tavern and four more will take any location, you need at least five green taverns. Knowing which quests can be active together is hard, and knowing how likely that is harder still, so Horneman's team assumed the worst case: the player takes every optional quest and never finishes any ([Jurie Horneman 2023, 14:06](https://youtu.be/FV_0rmqxbxw?t=846)).
3. **Watch for repetition the rules allow.** Tag-based selection can work exactly as designed and still show the player the same quest again and again, because the tag constraints combine with how content is spread through the world to make one option very likely. His example is a bard who keeps getting the same ointment quest because it is tagged for an enemy type the player happens to meet often. Repetition caused by distribution like this is much harder to spot in the data than a plain bug ([Jurie Horneman 2023, 14:57](https://youtu.be/FV_0rmqxbxw?t=897)).

### Letting the player set the parameters

Robin Sloan reverses the usual flow: the player defines the quest and the machine writes it. He generated and mailed about a thousand GPT-2 fantasy quest stories, each set up by a reader's survey answers and tied to its own generated map. The fiction is an academy of wizards simulating possible quests against a Dark Lord; letters were styled as crusty mainframe reports and sent through a mailing API, and every quest ends in defeat. He suggests a play-by-mail game is waiting to be built this way ([Robin Sloan 2019, 3:51](https://youtu.be/cIpErjWBqm0?t=231)). The survey offered preset options next to free-text fields (who leads the quest; what they seek, from a sword to a severed head; what they meet, from an elk to a melancholy giant) so that readers who did not feel creative could still set up a quest. The resulting file of inputs, from a theologian to a swarm of ticks, was a delight in itself ([Robin Sloan 2019, 5:56](https://youtu.be/cIpErjWBqm0?t=356)).

## Casting events: storylets, plots and oracles

A lot of narrative generation is not invention. It is choosing which piece of authored content fits the current situation, and deciding who plays which part. Several independent systems converge on this model: write a library of small events with conditions (and, in two of them, roles), then select and cast ([Patrick Belanger and Jackson Wagner 2025, 8:52](https://youtu.be/vtU3Xa0ShKw?t=532); [Max Kreminski 2017, 5:08](https://youtu.be/66O6WDcT8KY?t=308); [Paris Buttfield-Addison 2026, 6:37:15](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=23835)). The alternative, which comes from solo tabletop play, gives the player an abstract prompt and lets them do the inventing.

### A library of plays

Patrick Belanger and Jackson Wagner describe Wildermyth's random events as a "library of plays" in which the heroes are the cast. The game picks events whose roles the current party can fill, and weights more specific events higher. An event with a wolf hero talking to a parent in a forest scores higher than generic friends chatting, so the party gets the event that best fits who they are, with the aim of acknowledging the heroes and pushing them toward who they could become ([Patrick Belanger and Jackson Wagner 2025, 8:52](https://youtu.be/vtU3Xa0ShKw?t=532)).

Roles are filled by scoring candidates. One event picks a second hero who is the friend or lover of the first, preferring lovers, then a third with the highest leader stat among those left. Events can also filter on overland tile, site, party and foes. Optional roles let extra content trigger, such as a choice that appears only if there is a lover ([Patrick Belanger and Jackson Wagner 2025, 11:26](https://youtu.be/vtU3Xa0ShKw?t=686)). The role names are only labels:

> Note hero, friend and leader are just names we are giving the roles. It doesn't matter the name. The logic is happening in the scoring. — [Patrick Belanger and Jackson Wagner 2025, 11:26](https://youtu.be/vtU3Xa0ShKw?t=686)

Max Kreminski's Star Freighter uses the same structure with a term borrowed from Failbetter's Fallen London: *storylets*, small self-contained story units with prerequisites. Unlike Fallen London, where the player chooses, Star Freighter picks dynamically from the storylets whose prerequisites are currently met. One example selects two crew members who have not recently had a very bad interaction, writes the scene with a text grammar, and gives each a memory of a slightly better relationship ([Max Kreminski 2017, 5:08](https://youtu.be/66O6WDcT8KY?t=308)). Kreminski adds the casting idea's long-term half: Star Freighter keeps every generated character in its database and brings them back in new roles. Defeated bounty hunters often survive to return, former passengers turn up again, and merchants track reputation, so backtracking has consequences. Throwing characters away after one fight or quest limits how far they can develop; he compares the result to Shadow of Mordor's nemesis system generalised to every character ([Max Kreminski 2017, 12:25](https://youtu.be/66O6WDcT8KY?t=745)).

Selection by specificity can also reproduce a classic roguelike feature. Paris Buttfield-Addison shows that *salience* selection (picking the content whose conditions best match the current state) can implement bones, the leftover remains of a previous dead character. In his demo roguelike, Dungeons of Mild Peril, rooms are a pool and the bones room, which records a dead character's floor, name and gold, has one extra condition: it only qualifies on the floor where you died. That makes it score higher than ordinary rooms, so it usually wins a tie, but a less-seen room still goes first, so bones are likely, not guaranteed. He notes they are not guaranteed in NetHack either ([Paris Buttfield-Addison 2026, 6:37:15](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=23835)).

Smaller designs use the same move with less machinery. Dungeon Court, a party game by Randy Lubin and Raph D'Amico, randomly pairs plaintiffs and defendants from a printed deck of monsters and heroes with pre-written cases. Each player gets a card describing their side, and the drawn character supplies traits such as a smelly, gregarious blob, which gives players scaffolding so they do not come to the case cold ([Randy Lubin and Raph D'Amico 2019, 5:34](https://youtu.be/ftSC3Sn8O_s?t=334)). Nathan Savant suggests assigning each NPC a motivation from a list when it is generated and keying dialogue and reactions to that motivation, so characters talk about their current goals or their history with the player ([Nathan Savant 2026, 8:25](https://youtu.be/rmddpcmIJ2I?t=505)).

### Plots that guarantee payoff

Selection on its own does not guarantee a story holds together. Jasmine Otto's *cyclic plot generation* borrows from cyclic dungeon generation as used in Unexplored, where the generator guarantees that every locked door has a key. Otto's version guarantees that every plot element that is set up will pay off. She colours a social graph with roles (an heir who generates a verb toward a target, plus a helper) and reads the plot off the colouring. Each verb may change state in the world, while its storylet is a prose gloss whose consequences exist only in the reader's mind ([Jasmine Otto 2021, 10:21](https://youtu.be/NjIDVIIg1lY?t=621)). The guarantee has an odd consequence: because characters must complete their remaining actions, a character who is killed cannot simply be removed. Otto changes their deck so they come back as a ghost, and other characters react with suitable distress, which she calls fun to write for ([Jasmine Otto 2021, 12:55](https://youtu.be/NjIDVIIg1lY?t=775)).

Ian Holmes used a graph grammar, the same approach he used for dungeons, to generate a choose-your-own-adventure story graph: mostly tree-like but with local cycles, ending in outcomes such as a boss or death, all from a very small set of rules. The appeal, he says, is that a compact rule set is easy to understand, analyse, debug and maintain ([Ian Holmes 2017, 15:58](https://youtu.be/b2VkgcC1xRc?t=958)).

### Oracles: prompts the player interprets

Solo tabletop roleplaying solves a related problem without authored events at all. Cezar Capacle explains how an *oracle* replaces the game master. Yes/no questions ("is it raining?") are answered by dice or cards modified by how likely the answer is. Open questions (what, where, why, how) are answered by random words that, like tarot cards, have no predefined meaning; the player interprets them in context. A treasure table, by contrast, would have to anticipate every interaction the players might have ([Cezar Capacle 2024, 5:11](https://youtu.be/NklQJfhZT3k?t=311)).

The interpretation step is what ties output to the particular story. Capacle's example uses the meaning tables of Mythic Game Master Emulator to roll "heal" and "fear" for what is in a chest. Read plainly, that is a potion that cures fear. For a character afraid of mimics, though, opening an empty chest safely could be the moment they overcome that fear ([Cezar Capacle 2024, 7:59](https://youtu.be/NklQJfhZT3k?t=479)).

Oracles are not unshaped randomness. Capacle says they can be curated toward a theme even though they give no fixed results. Where a treasure table says "100 gold pieces, five sapphires", an item oracle might pair magic-effect words (transparent, void, fire) with mishap words (corruption, decay, metamorphosis) to define both an item's power and the risk of misusing it ([Cezar Capacle 2024, 27:29](https://youtu.be/NklQJfhZT3k?t=1649)). A *complication oracle* sits between pure random words and fixed complication lists: a few evocative verbs (break, harm, lose, escalate, drain, expose) with guiding keywords. Rolling "escalate" on a failed lock-pick can become guards hearing a noise and dismissing it, which adds tension without derailing the mission. It produces complications you would not have thought of, without repeating ([Cezar Capacle 2024, 19:05](https://youtu.be/NklQJfhZT3k?t=1145)).

Getting the words right is slow. Capacle cites Avery Alder's remark that design can be hours spent arriving at a list of 12 words. He gathered about 200 candidate words from published games, videos and Reddit and cut them to six, discarding any that were too similar, too broad or too specific. By his account, curating six words for a random table takes a week ([Cezar Capacle 2024, 30:08](https://youtu.be/NklQJfhZT3k?t=1808)).

### Choosing between selection and interpretation

The two approaches put the authoring in different places. With a library of plays or storylets, you write the prose and the conditions, and the generator's skill lies in matching: specificity weights, role scoring, reuse of characters, and guarantees of payoff ([Patrick Belanger and Jackson Wagner 2025, 8:52](https://youtu.be/vtU3Xa0ShKw?t=532); [Max Kreminski 2017, 12:25](https://youtu.be/66O6WDcT8KY?t=745); [Jasmine Otto 2021, 10:21](https://youtu.be/NjIDVIIg1lY?t=621)). The player sees finished, authored text. With an oracle, you write a small, carefully pitched vocabulary, and the player's imagination does the matching ([Cezar Capacle 2024, 5:11](https://youtu.be/NklQJfhZT3k?t=311); [Cezar Capacle 2024, 30:08](https://youtu.be/NklQJfhZT3k?t=1808)). A computer game cannot rely on the player to narrate as a solo tabletop player does, but the oracle lessons still apply to any prompt-like content: pitch it at the right level of abstraction, curate it toward a theme, and give it a specific job such as complications.

## Generated puzzles, riddles and traps

Josh Galecki states the problem plainly. Roguelikes are built on repetition, and a puzzle does not survive repetition:

> Solving a puzzle once is fun. Solving it twice is trivial. And solving it for the 20th time is a chore. — [Josh Galecki 2023, 1:46](https://youtu.be/6vMxH6OtI54?t=106)

So in a roguelike, puzzles have to come from puzzle *systems* that produce new instances on demand. Galecki built Moondrop, a nonviolent farming roguelike, around this, using puzzles instead of combat as the challenge in its dungeons ([Josh Galecki 2023, 1:46](https://youtu.be/6vMxH6OtI54?t=106)). The two most detailed systems in the talks reach the same answer by different routes: make the puzzle out of many pieces of information that refer to each other, and make the player find the answer by cross-referencing them.

### Riddles in a generated world

Mark R Johnson's Ultima Ratio Regum, whose per-culture names appear earlier in the chapter, generates complete multi-step pilgrimage riddles. In his demo a priest points to a wall inscription and a swordsmith's cryptic note; deciphering them leads to a granary in a town named for the sky and to a tavern basement wall facing the slum in a city named for a cold hand. Every component, from the holy book to the reward relic (a goblet from a system of tens of thousands), was generated, and the whole chain is unique to that playthrough ([Mark Johnson 2023, 20:08](https://youtu.be/RDWt6RGN9wM?t=1208)).

Johnson's design rules follow from the size of the world, which has around 2.5 billion tiles, dozens of nations and hundreds of settlements. A single linear chain would fail, because the player might never find its first link. Instead, each riddle needs many scattered lead-ins (NPCs, books, places, times) converging on pieces that refer to one another. New games start with simple clues about the player's home nation, but beyond that, multiple ways in are, in his words, extremely important ([Mark Johnson 2023, 26:05](https://youtu.be/RDWt6RGN9wM?t=1565)). The generator works in two passes. First it builds a chain of *checkpoints*, points at which the player has enough information to move on; then it distributes each checkpoint's clues into media such as inscriptions, books, dialogue, statues or secret rooms. Johnson admits it does not yet check that the links make sense (why would a priest point to a merchant?) and wants a more logical chain in future ([Mark Johnson 2023, 34:52](https://youtu.be/RDWt6RGN9wM?t=2092)).

Two properties of the world make this possible. The first is cross-referencing: consistent aesthetics for each civilisation, and books and NPCs that mention other people, places and books, so the player can work things out rather than be told, with as many ways as possible into each chain, while every required piece is actually generated and reachable ([Mark Johnson 2023, 25:00](https://youtu.be/RDWt6RGN9wM?t=1500)). The second is *referability*. Things need enough describable variation to be picked out (his generated statues of gods and historical figures have billions of permutations) and many alternative names, so that clues can point at them indirectly. One city in the demo is referred to in many different ways, and references can span several levels, like a clue about a king's "bane" that you can only resolve by reading another book, not by guessing synonyms ([Mark Johnson 2023, 23:06](https://youtu.be/RDWt6RGN9wM?t=1386)).

### Corrupted databases

Bjarke Alexander Larsen's Telegrams from the Quiet Train, a puzzle game run in a Discord bot, gets repeatable logic puzzles from a different source. The lore says a distorting force corrupted all stored text, so the game derives 13 corrupted databases from a hidden ground truth, each giving a different version (four possible addresses for one name, say). Players start from a trusted recipient ID and cross-reference databases, accepting an answer once several sources agree. Larsen's walkthrough finds an address that appears in both the voting registry and the commuting registry, then confirms it with two more databases ([Bjarke Alexander Larsen 2026, 4:43](https://youtu.be/gxXZRofE5dI?t=283)).

Two design choices keep it from collapsing into brute force. Each database maps different fields (names to jobs, work addresses to home addresses), and each is corrupted in its own characteristic way: some only add wrong answers, so the right one is always present, while others shuffle more or are more corrupted. Players learn the "texture" of each source, how trustworthy and how useful it is, and querying everything becomes less attractive ([Bjarke Alexander Larsen 2026, 10:23](https://youtu.be/gxXZRofE5dI?t=623)). And each order starts from an ID that reveals a different subset of information. Starting with a name and a job leads through different databases than starting with a home address and district, which gives each instance its own path through the web. Larsen calls this key to keeping instances fresh over a long-running game ([Bjarke Alexander Larsen 2026, 11:33](https://youtu.be/gxXZRofE5dI?t=693)).

The convergence between Johnson and Larsen is the main lesson of this section. Both make a puzzle out of many partial sources that refer to the same hidden facts, and both vary where the player comes in ([Mark Johnson 2023, 26:05](https://youtu.be/RDWt6RGN9wM?t=1565); [Bjarke Alexander Larsen 2026, 11:33](https://youtu.be/gxXZRofE5dI?t=693)). Neither generates a puzzle shape and then decorates it; both generate a body of consistent information and let the puzzle be finding your way through it.

### Trap patterns

Sersa Victory and Joris Dormans make a related argument about traps. The tables of specific traps in RPG supplements do not say what makes a trap interesting. Generic, reusable trap *patterns*, in the sense of software or UI design patterns, describe the underlying interactions and so give designers and generators a vocabulary for modelling, combining and generating them, which a generator can then reify into any theme ([Sersa Victory and Joris Dormans 2026, 7:26](https://youtu.be/NjIduRLJL7U?t=446)). Their patterns "unfold" across time and space, which puts demands on the generator: it must know the larger dungeon's room order and contents, and the thematic ways elements can interact. Acid corrodes armour and burns stone; a sarcophagus can contain a mummy; a mummy can move to another room. Each abstract pattern has to be translated into relationships between concrete elements like these ([Sersa Victory and Joris Dormans 2026, 14:57](https://youtu.be/NjIduRLJL7U?t=897)).

### Smaller cases

- **Puzzles generated from generated text.** Kingdom of Loathing has a 1,500-line script by writer Riff Conner that generates a fake game FAQ for an imaginary video game and then builds a playable zone from it, including a maze you can only solve by reading the FAQ. The scripting language, made so writers could code without PHP, could set persistent state on the player, which is what let the generated text feed back into play. Zack Johnson calls it the culmination of the game's text generation ([Zack Johnson 2016, 17:43](https://youtu.be/jNUMRG_tvrY?t=1063)).
- **Randomised answers against the wiki.** Kingdom of Loathing's original endgame had a lock guarded by a liar, a truth-teller and one who craves human flesh, giving clues to a randomly generated code. Zack Johnson says the point was to stop players looking it up: if the answer is just a number, it can be any number ([Zack Johnson 2016, 20:01](https://youtu.be/jNUMRG_tvrY?t=1201)).
- **Mysteries from simple rules.** Leigh Alexander's McMansion places a random set of celebrities in a fixed-layout mansion with randomly generated room images and secretly makes one the murderer, who kills anyone left alone with them. Opportunity is the main clue, and items such as a knife or a pool noodle are tied to the murder method ([Leigh Alexander 2023, 10:11](https://youtu.be/NjYS8XmeaiY?t=611)).
- **Mazes with a purpose.** Andrew Plotkin notes that a maze can earn its place if the sequence of landmarks along its path becomes a clue later ([Andrew Plotkin 2026, 21:23](https://youtu.be/7h3T5NaFpcI?t=1283)). Logic mazes, which add a rule such as alternating colours or only turning left, make good puzzles, but because the same square can be in a different state depending on colour or facing, the rule distances the player from the feeling of finding their way in space ([Andrew Plotkin 2026, 22:25](https://youtu.be/7h3T5NaFpcI?t=1345)).
- **Borrowed mathematics.** Galecki sources Moondrop's puzzles from interesting maths problems, especially graph theory, then gives them a theme that fits a cozy game, such as fishing and a river grid on the damp trail ([Josh Galecki 2023, 14:07](https://youtu.be/6vMxH6OtI54?t=847)).
- **Accidental puzzles.** In Chogue, a chess roguelike, late levels sometimes generate real chess problems, such as two remaining pieces facing three queens and two rooks. Jonathan Lessard says they first imagined the game as generated chess problems in arbitrary spaces and suggests generated or player-made chess-problem dungeons as further work ([Jonathan Lessard 2018, 30:39](https://youtu.be/l1YEJBKehAY?t=1839)).
- **The unknown monster.** Todd Furmanski proposes generating the monster itself, so the player, like a horror-movie character, must find out what works against it: do bullets work on a vampire you can only see in mirrors? ([Todd Furmanski 2020, 21:05](https://youtu.be/ST6s_8ekeOg?t=1265)) He frames the same idea for a haunted house where you know there is a monster but not whether it is a vampire or a werewolf, alongside open-ended puzzles like decoding a library in an unknown language through context ([Darren Grey et al. 2020, 36:50](https://youtu.be/tmrYfnMrifw?t=2210)).

### Keeping generated puzzles fair

The talks suggest a short set of rules for generated puzzles that the player can solve by deduction:

- **Generate the truth first, then the clues.** Larsen derives every database from a hidden ground truth, and Mark R Johnson builds the checkpoint chain before distributing clues ([Bjarke Alexander Larsen 2026, 4:43](https://youtu.be/gxXZRofE5dI?t=283); [Mark Johnson 2023, 34:52](https://youtu.be/RDWt6RGN9wM?t=2092)).
- **Guarantee every required piece exists and can be reached.** Johnson pairs cross-referencing with making sure every required piece is actually generated and accessible ([Mark Johnson 2023, 25:00](https://youtu.be/RDWt6RGN9wM?t=1500)).
- **Give more than one way in.** Scattered lead-ins and varied starting information keep a puzzle findable and each instance different ([Mark Johnson 2023, 26:05](https://youtu.be/RDWt6RGN9wM?t=1565); [Bjarke Alexander Larsen 2026, 11:33](https://youtu.be/gxXZRofE5dI?t=693)).
- **Make sources learnable.** Consistent corruption textures and consistent civilisation aesthetics let the player build judgement over time ([Bjarke Alexander Larsen 2026, 10:23](https://youtu.be/gxXZRofE5dI?t=623); [Mark Johnson 2023, 25:00](https://youtu.be/RDWt6RGN9wM?t=1500)).
- **Check that links make sense.** Johnson names illogical links as his generator's open weakness ([Mark Johnson 2023, 34:52](https://youtu.be/RDWt6RGN9wM?t=2092)).
- **Give the generator knowledge of interactions.** Traps that unfold need to know room order and what elements can do to each other ([Sersa Victory and Joris Dormans 2026, 14:57](https://youtu.be/NjIduRLJL7U?t=897)).

## The meaning players make: attachment, apophenia and unintended readings

The earlier sections treat generated content from the generator's side. This one looks from the player's side. Players read meaning into generated output, and they do it whether or not you intended any. That is how a list of names becomes a cast people love, and it is also how a flower becomes an offensive symbol ([Elliot Trinidad 2023, 4:28](https://youtu.be/9yFferxbrBU?t=268); [Younès Rabii 2020, 8:01](https://youtu.be/s6Kxh_Zyiqs?t=481)).

### Incongruity invites interpretation

Florence Smith Nicholls argues that incongruity and ambiguity push players to interpret game worlds, and that the uncanny texture of procedural generation, its repetitions and glitches, is the same kind of prompt. From her study she derives "archaeological game world affordances", qualities that make players interpret more or extend an interpretation, and suggests having players record or make artifacts that interpret what they find in generated worlds ([Florence Smith Nicholls 2025, 8:15](https://youtu.be/9kqvF2TqxLo?t=495)).

Younès Rabii describes the same process in his Tea Garden, a generator of flowers. It works like cloud-gazing: around 90% of the flowers carry no meaning for any player, but the rest evoke something players recognise and grow attached to, and different players see different things. An orange flower is just orange; a pink one looks like a butterfly; a green one looks like a frog's face and is his favourite, because it is round and lovable ([Younès Rabii 2020, 3:47](https://youtu.be/s6Kxh_Zyiqs?t=227)). Notice the ratio. You do not need every output to mean something, only enough that players keep looking. This fits the earlier argument about baselines and spikes.

### Attachment from very little

Two talks about Blaseball, by different speakers, show how little a player needs to become attached to generated content. Blaseball's randomly generated players had no graphics, only names and a few facts such as a favourite coffee, yet fans formed deep attachments and made art and fiction about them. Elliot Trinidad links this to the game's unscripted outcomes, which made chance events feel like miracles ([Elliot Trinidad 2023, 4:28](https://youtu.be/9yFferxbrBU?t=268)). Joel Clark, who made the game partly because he likes generating fake names and getting attached to them, says players became far more attached to the generated players and teams than the developers expected, and fan art of them surprised him ([Joel Clark 2020, 30:32](https://youtu.be/zO05p-e57AQ?t=1832)).

Randomness can make a character feel more personal, not less. Shawn Main recalls the random tables of Palladium's Heroes Unlimited, which covered origins, powers and backstory down to how many disguises you own. He rolled that he was an alien and ended up a doglike person from an ice planet with electricity powers: a character he would never have come up with, and which felt more his for it ([Shawn Main 2017, 2:30](https://youtu.be/UZ7XqQYDM7o?t=150)). Seven Day Band, a 7DRL (a roguelike made in seven days), takes this furthest by having the player author the content during play. You meet unknown enemies and objects and set their names and abilities when you first encounter them or when they start to matter, through an occasional menu rather than a long setup screen ([Josh Ge 2018, 8:57](https://youtu.be/jviNpRGuCIU?t=537)).

### You cannot control what it means

The other side of interpretation is that you cannot fully control it. Rabii gave one of his flowers, a blue-and-pink T shape, a positive reading as trans rights activism; the same generator also produced cross-shaped flowers with four branches that looked to him like fascist imagery. There is no easy way to prevent such readings, so designers have to ask what they want their game to be able to evoke. Generated content can unsettle even its developer: he once found a skull in a garden while debugging ([Younès Rabii 2020, 8:01](https://youtu.be/s6Kxh_Zyiqs?t=481)). Alexandra Leonhart, citing Mike Cook's essay in *Procedural Storytelling in Game Design*, asks designers to consider whether their procedural systems' intent is readable to a diverse audience, because algorithms produce unintended outcomes that players read as statements. Cook's example is how generated names on gravestones imply who is allowed in a space ([Alexandra Leonhart 2026, 8:29:07](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=30547)).

### Safeguards

The talks offer concrete practices, mostly from Blaseball and from Darius Kazemi's text bots:

- **Audit the pool for who it represents.** Blaseball felt global in its fiction and its fan base, but the characters it generated did not, because online English-speaking fandoms default to a white American perspective. Trinidad made fixing that a high priority because, even though names do not touch mechanics, they shape how the community interacts and attaches to characters. Investing in an anti-racist fandom, he says, yields an easier community ([Elliot Trinidad 2023, 16:13](https://youtu.be/9yFferxbrBU?t=973)).
- **Retire names that have become famous.** Blaseball retired names already tied to well-known characters, like retiring a jersey number. A second Parker in the same season would be a funny coincidence; one a year later would be distracting and would stop the new character being their own person ([Elliot Trinidad 2023, 12:46](https://youtu.be/9yFferxbrBU?t=766)).
- **Treat name lists as living documents.** A Blaseball surname matched a famous football player who made offensive comments about Black Lives Matter in 2020. Fans asked for a change and the team made it at no cost. Trinidad also recommends hiring sensitivity consultants when you draw on real cultures ([Elliot Trinidad 2023, 26:37](https://youtu.be/9yFferxbrBU?t=1597)).
- **Filter in layers and publish a takedown policy.** Kazemi uses a shared word-filter module, per-bot blacklists, and targeted detectors: for Two Headlines he built a subsystem that detects transphobic jokes in a generated tweet and deletes them before posting. He accepts that you will never catch everything, so he also publishes a policy and deletes on report ([Darius Kazemi 2017, 32:32](https://youtu.be/CLi4PWxDmAI?t=1952)).

These are layers, not a cure. Rabii's point stands that there is no easy way to prevent every reading ([Younès Rabii 2020, 8:01](https://youtu.be/s6Kxh_Zyiqs?t=481)). What you can do is reduce the obvious failures before release and respond quickly after.

### When the unintended reading is the good part

Not every unintended output is a problem to fix. Jason Grinblat recalls Jeremiah Reid's time-travel roguelike, in which marriage had not been disabled on death, so characters kept marrying the deceased and the logs filled with weddings. Grinblat's response was to wonder what game would take that bug seriously as its premise. He also mentions Caves of Qud's weekly bug triage, opened to Discord helpers, where bug reports often read like poetry, and the Dwarf Fortress fix log as an archive of beautiful bugs ([Jason Grinblat 2021, 30:57](https://youtu.be/kvCky6BbTuE?t=1857)). Qud's own Mehmet fight, described under generated history, shows how close the call can be: Grinblat counts it a big gameplay leak, because it locks players out of the starting side quest ([Jason Grinblat 2021, 19:47](https://youtu.be/kvCky6BbTuE?t=1187)), but he also values what it teaches players about the game's systems and calls it even money whether the team fixes it. Before you fix a strange output, ask whether players would find meaning in it.

## Tensions and open questions

**Breadth or restraint?** George Moromisato credits NetHack's endurance to the sheer breadth of its monsters and things to do, and Jon Perry's Mini and Max needed rewards everywhere to keep its promise ([George Moromisato 2016, 25:05](https://youtu.be/QBZkvtGucBU?t=1505); [Jon Perry 2025, 7:14](https://youtu.be/NlxGPKV0PrY?t=434)). Against them, Bruno Dias says generation does not multiply cheap content, Cole Wehrle keeps Oath's play deck small so players form relationships with particular cards, and Rich Wilson warns of the "threat of infinite content" ([Bruno Dias 2016, 11:49](https://youtu.be/UGPkEWqwSAY?t=709); [Cole Wehrle 2025, 19:31](https://youtu.be/HgnvMBVKP0M?t=1171); [Rich Wilson 2021, 11:22](https://youtu.be/wtlLa7BGZcs?t=682)). Max Kreminski adds an ethical edge, that endless content can feed an extractive mode of play ([Max Kreminski 2018, 12:19](https://youtu.be/TvlZinAvpwg?t=739)). The camps differ less than they seem: what decides it is whether each added piece gives the player something distinct they can recognise and care about, and whether you want players to know your content deeply or keep meeting the new.

**Consistency or swings?** Evan Debenham's interleaved loot decks in Shattered Pixel Dungeon smooth out runs, preventing cases like an early player finding four of the same armour type when only the first is useful ([Evan Debenham 2022, 8:10](https://youtu.be/kaojiu9syPE?t=490)); John Harris counts the first Shiren's willingness to hand out great items early, transforming a run, as one of the best reasons to play it ([John Harris 2024, 14:18](https://youtu.be/0MdNwIHwXy0?t=858)). The choice depends on whether your game's variety comes from steady build decisions or from adapting to rare windfalls.

**Show the machinery or hide it?** Cole Wehrle disagrees with himself, productively. Random tables expose the whole generative space, which he loves, but understanding how they work undoes the illusion ([Cole Wehrle 2025, 8:47](https://youtu.be/HgnvMBVKP0M?t=527)); Tales of the Arabian Nights hides a simple structure behind layers of lookup and feels like an open world ([Cole Wehrle 2025, 9:35](https://youtu.be/HgnvMBVKP0M?t=575)); yet too much obfuscation becomes white noise ([Cole Wehrle 2025, 10:21](https://youtu.be/HgnvMBVKP0M?t=621)). The talks give no formula for the right amount of indirection. The test Wehrle implies is whether each outcome still carries intention once the player can no longer see the dice.

**Templates or language models?** Robin Sloan argues a template's seams show after about five reads, so language-model output lasts longer ([Robin Sloan 2019, 18:33](https://youtu.be/cIpErjWBqm0?t=1113)). Ada Null finds a simple, low-variation grammar enough for Kiss Garden, because its narrator lets the text blur together ([Ada Null 2025, 6:18](https://youtu.be/VzoruhRyvqQ?t=378)). Brianna McHorse and Chris Foster say language models lack the consistency over time that games need, and carry ethical risks ([Brianna McHorse and Chris Foster 2023, 15:30](https://youtu.be/aJC3ioashbs?t=930); [Brianna McHorse and Chris Foster 2023, 11:24](https://youtu.be/aJC3ioashbs?t=684)). What decides between them is whether the text must stay consistent with game state across a run, and whether readers will see enough outputs to notice the pattern.

**Generated phonology or curated lists?** Sraëka-Lillian and Mark R Johnson generate the rules of each culture's names, and Johnson reassigns naming archetypes every world ([Sraëka-Lillian 2021, 1:37](https://youtu.be/XQKNwaCwD-I?t=97); [Mark R Johnson 2019, 17:09](https://youtu.be/qh9vyoMviJI?t=1029)); Elliot Trinidad's Blaseball picks a random first and last name from curated lists and puts the effort into curation ([Elliot Trinidad 2023, 8:24](https://youtu.be/9yFferxbrBU?t=504)). Neither talk frames it this way, but the choice appears to turn on whether your cultures are invented per world or fixed.

**Flavour or balance?** Dustin Freeman regrets Stellaris removing its distinct faster-than-light methods for balance, valuing the evocativeness of an asymmetric universe over its fairness ([Dustin Freeman 2020, 6:21](https://youtu.be/8HDmpu7Kp-A?t=381)). That is one designer's preference; a game whose players compete with each other may weigh it differently.

**Authored-then-selected or interpreted?** Wildermyth's library of plays and Star Freighter's storylets put the authoring in the prose and the matching in the generator ([Patrick Belanger and Jackson Wagner 2025, 8:52](https://youtu.be/vtU3Xa0ShKw?t=532); [Max Kreminski 2017, 5:08](https://youtu.be/66O6WDcT8KY?t=308)); Cezar Capacle's oracles give the player a few evocative words and leave the interpreting to them ([Cezar Capacle 2024, 5:11](https://youtu.be/NklQJfhZT3k?t=311)). A computer game cannot assume a player will narrate, so how far oracle-style prompts can carry a digital roguelike remains open.

**How much can you control?** Younès Rabii says there is no easy way to prevent every reading of generated output ([Younès Rabii 2020, 8:01](https://youtu.be/s6Kxh_Zyiqs?t=481)); Elliot Trinidad and Darius Kazemi offer layered safeguards that reduce the obvious failures and respond quickly to the rest ([Elliot Trinidad 2023, 16:13](https://youtu.be/9yFferxbrBU?t=973); [Elliot Trinidad 2023, 26:37](https://youtu.be/9yFferxbrBU?t=1597); [Darius Kazemi 2017, 32:32](https://youtu.be/CLi4PWxDmAI?t=1952)). And Jason Grinblat suggests that some unintended outputs are worth keeping as premises ([Jason Grinblat 2021, 30:57](https://youtu.be/kvCky6BbTuE?t=1857)). Where a strange output falls between harm and delight is a judgment the talks leave to the designer.

**Unsolved problems.** Several speakers name problems they have not cracked:

- Mark R Johnson's riddle generator does not yet check that its links make sense ([Mark Johnson 2023, 34:52](https://youtu.be/RDWt6RGN9wM?t=2092)).
- Jason Grinblat needs a hand-made secret generator for each kind of lore and wants a general way to turn procedural elements into Markov-ready secrets ([Jason Grinblat 2016, 22:58](https://youtu.be/zDTQM0Ipiz4?t=1378)).
- Kate Compton has no good way to handle grammatical gender in Tracery ([Kate Compton 2016, 31:09](https://youtu.be/isB82kORimk?t=1869)).
- Ben Berman calls functional content, such as monster behaviours and playable cards, the next frontier ([Ben Berman 2017, 29:29](https://youtu.be/Z6lHExfem6U?t=1769)).
- Liza Knipscher's Bioloom crossover keeps a parent's parts but loses where they were placed ([Liza Knipscher 2025, 13:49](https://youtu.be/jBhcHdV5HHo?t=829)).
- Mark Gritter's economies have no triangle trades, transport costs or geography yet ([Mark Gritter 2020, 9:28](https://youtu.be/Q_MFTUYnaf0?t=568)).
- Ezra Szanton's real-world network deckbuilder still needs a rule set that turns a network's qualities into play ([Ezra Szanton 2025, 26:23](https://youtu.be/JfNeYtH7xI4?t=1583)).
- Jurie Horneman warns that repetition caused by the distribution of content is much harder to spot in data than a bug ([Jurie Horneman 2023, 14:57](https://youtu.be/FV_0rmqxbxw?t=897)).

## Checklist

1. Can a player perceive the difference between two outputs of each generator, and does that difference change what they do?
2. Are any attributes generated independently that should be correlated or bundled, so that one region differs from the next?
3. Does each region, society or town have one organising idea that colours everything in it?
4. Is your baseline deliberately plain, and is your rare tail set by explicit tiers or percentages tuned to how many items the player will see?
5. For each pool, have you decided whether to draw with or without replacement?
6. Is every generator fed by enough authored material, and would a smaller, themed space serve better than a bigger one?
7. Is your content authored in structures (tags, variants, category matrices) that let one entry multiply into many and flow into every system?
8. Does your text generator know anything about its fragments, such as tone, length or theme, and could that become characterization?
9. Where does your generated text come from, and does that source have the voice you want?
10. Do your name generators give each culture a recognisable, consistent identity?
11. Does every generated history, system or quest leave a trace the player can find and act on?
12. Have you written down the context and purpose of your quest generator, and checked that your allocator can never run out of valid locations?
13. Can each generated puzzle be solved by deduction, with the truth generated first and more than one way in?
14. Have you audited your generated pools for whom they represent, and do you have a way to filter, change and take down output after release?
15. When a generator produces something strange, do you ask whether players would find meaning in it before you fix it?
